description: Western Hindi variety closely related to Khariboli.

name: Sindhi
description: Northwestern Indo-Aryan language; preserves implosive consonants; written in Perso-Arabic (Pakistan) and Devanagari (India). Scheduled language of India and provincial language of Sindh.

name: Kachchhi (Kutchi)
description: Indo-Aryan language often classified as a Sindhi variety though with strong Gujarati contact features.

name: Saraiki (Siraiki)
description: Northwestern Indo-Aryan (Lahnda) variety; close to Punjabi but with distinct phonology (implosives) and morphology.

name: Hindko
description: Lahnda variety in Pashto-dominated regions; Peshawari Hindko has urban prestige tradition.

name: Pothohari
description: Lahnda variety often grouped under western Punjabi.

name: Konkani
description: Indo-Aryan language with literary tradition; scheduled language of India; written in Devanagari, Roman, Kannada, and Malayalam scripts depending on community.

name: Dogri
description: Pahari Indo-Aryan language; scheduled language of India since 2003.

name: Bhili (macrolanguage)
description: Indo-Aryan macrolanguage cluster of the Bhil tribal peoples; multiple varieties (Wagdi, Vasavi, Bhilali, etc.).

name: Dhivehi (Maldivian)
description: Indo-Aryan language closely related to Sinhala but separated by ~1000 years of divergence; written in the right-to-left Thaana script (developed 18th c.).

name: Rohingya
region: Rakhine State (Myanmar) and refugee camps in Bangladesh
description: Eastern Indo-Aryan language closely related to Chittagonian Bengali; written in the Hanifi Rohingya script (developed 1980s).

name: Saurashtra
description: Indo-Aryan language preserved by silk-weaver community that migrated from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu in the late medieval period.

name: Chittagonian
description: Eastern Indo-Aryan language; typically grouped with Bengali but not mutually intelligible with Standard Bengali.

name: Sylheti
region: Sylhet Division (Bangladesh) and Barak Valley (Assam, India)
description: Eastern Indo-Aryan language historically written in the indigenous Sylheti Nagri script (revived); status as Bengali dialect vs separate language is socially contested.

name: Garhwali
description: Central Pahari Indo-Aryan language.

name: Kumaoni
description: Central Pahari Indo-Aryan language.

name: Shina
region: Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan; Indus Kohistan; Drass and Gurez, India
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language.

name: Khowar
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language; one of few Indo-Aryan languages outside the main subcontinent.

name: Kohistani (Indus Kohistani)
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language.

name: Kalasha
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language of the non-Muslim Kalasha people; preserves archaic Indo-Aryan features.

name: Pashai
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language cluster.

name: Torwali
description: Dardic Indo-Aryan language.

name: Kati (Bashgali)
description: Major Nuristani language. Nuristani is a third primary branch of Indo-Iranian (alongside Indo-Aryan and Iranian), not a subgroup of Indo-Aryan; placed under proto-indo-aryan here only because the dataset lacks a proto-Indo-Iranian node above proto-iranian and proto-indo-aryan.

name: Prasun (Wasi-weri)
description: Most divergent Nuristani language; see Kati note re: Nuristani branch placement.

name: Waigali (Kalasha-ala)
description: Nuristani language; see Kati note.

name: Ashkun
description: Nuristani language; see Kati note.

name: Tregami
description: Nuristani language; see Kati note.

name: Median
description: Old Iranian language of the Medes; not directly attested in continuous texts, reconstructed from loanwords in Old Persian and theonyms (e.g. zantu-, satrap-).

name: Parthian (Arsacid Pahlavi)
description: Northwestern Middle Iranian language of the Arsacid dynasty; attested in inscriptions, ostraca from Nisa, and Manichaean manuscripts from Turfan.

name: Bactrian
description: Middle Iranian language written in a modified Greek alphabet (introduced under Greco-Bactrians); used by the Kushan Empire; sole Iranian language so written. Extensively documented by the Rabatak inscription and the Bactrian Documents.

name: Khotanese Saka
description: Eastern Middle Iranian language attested in Buddhist manuscripts from Dunhuang and Khotan; written in Brahmi-derived script.

name: Tumshuqese Saka
description: Eastern Middle Iranian variety related to Khotanese; sparsely attested in a small corpus of manuscripts.

name: Khwarezmian (Chorasmian)
description: Eastern Middle Iranian language; attested in inscriptions on coins, legal documents, and glosses in Arabic juristic texts (Az-Zamakhsharī, Al-Bīrūnī) through the Islamic period.

name: Alanic (Old Ossetic)
description: Middle Iranian language of the Alans; sparse attestation including the Zelenchuk inscription (10th-12th c.); direct ancestor of modern Ossetic.

name: Sarmatian
description: Iranian language of the Sarmatians; not directly attested in continuous texts but reconstructed from personal and place names in Greek inscriptions of the Pontic colonies.

name: Zaza (Zazaki, Dimli)
description: Northwestern Iranian language spoken primarily by Alevi and Sunni Zaza populations; sometimes grouped with Gorani as 'Zaza-Gorani'.

name: Gorani (Hawrami)
description: Northwestern Iranian language; Hawrami variety is the historical literary language of the Ahl-e Haqq (Yarsani) religious tradition.

name: Mazandarani (Tabari)
description: Northwestern Iranian language of the Caspian coast; the Tabari literary tradition is one of the oldest in modern Iranian languages outside Persian (10th-c. attestations).

name: Gilaki
description: Northwestern Iranian language of the Caspian coast; closely related to Mazandarani.

name: Talysh
description: Northwestern Iranian language.

name: Tat (Muslim)
description: Southwestern Iranian language closely related to Persian; spoken by both Muslim Tats and Mountain Jews (whose variety is Judeo-Tat / Juhuri).

name: Judeo-Tat (Juhuri)
description: Jewish variety of Tat spoken by Mountain Jews; written historically in Hebrew script, later Cyrillic and Latin.

name: Semnani
description: Northwestern Iranian language cluster of north-central Iran.

name: Luri
description: Southwestern Iranian language cluster closely related to Persian; speakers number in millions but standardization is limited.

name: Bakhtiari
description: Luri variety associated with the Bakhtiari tribal confederation.

name: Lari (Achomi)
region: Fars, Iran (Lar, Bandar Abbas, Gulf coast)
description: Southwestern Iranian language often classed apart from standard Persian.

name: Kumzari
description: Sole Iranian language native to the Arabian Peninsula; descended from a southwestern Iranian source with strong Arabic contact.

name: Judeo-Persian
description: Persian language written in Hebrew script by Persian Jewish communities; among earliest New Persian texts (8th-c. Tang-i Azao inscription).

name: Hazaragi
description: Persian variety of the Hazara people; sometimes treated as a separate language; Mongolic loanwords.

name: Aimaq Persian
description: Persian variety of the Aimaq peoples.

name: Wakhi
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language; descended from a Saka-related Eastern Iranian source distinct from the rest of the Pamir group.

name: Yaghnobi
description: Northeastern Iranian language; sole surviving direct descendant of Sogdian.

name: Shughni
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language; largest of the Pamir languages.

name: Rushani
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language closely related to Shughni.

name: Yazghulami
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language.

name: Ishkashimi
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language.

name: Sanglechi
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language closely related to Ishkashimi.

name: Munji
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language.

name: Yidgha
description: Eastern Iranian Pamir language; closely related to Munji.

name: Ormuri
description: Southeastern Iranian language; severely endangered.

name: Parachi
description: Southeastern Iranian language; severely endangered.

name: Old French Sign Language (Vieux LSF)
description: Sign language used at the Institution Nationale des Sourds-Muets in Paris under the abbé de l'Épée and Sicard; ancestor of modern LSF and (via Laurent Clerc) of ASL. Differs from modern LSF in handshape inventory and grammar.

name: Martha's Vineyard Sign Language
description: Extinct village sign language used by both deaf and hearing islanders on Martha's Vineyard, where hereditary deafness was unusually common (~1 in 155 residents in some towns). Contributed signs and conventions to early ASL via Vineyard students at the American Asylum (1817).

name: Black American Sign Language
description: Sociolinguistic variety of ASL that diverged during the era of segregated deaf schools (post-1869 establishment of Black deaf schools). Documented systematic differences from mainstream ASL in handshape, two-handed signs, signing space, mouthing, and lexicon.

name: Puerto Rican Sign Language (LSPR)
description: ASL-derived sign language with substantial divergence; classification as separate language vs ASL variety is debated.

name: Bolivian Sign Language (LSB)
description: ASL-derived sign language introduced by American missionaries.

name: Filipino Sign Language (FSL)
description: ASL-derived sign language officially recognized as national sign language of the Philippines in 2018.

name: Malaysian Sign Language (BIM)
description: ASL-derived sign language.

name: Nigerian Sign Language
description: ASL-derived sign language introduced by deaf American missionary Andrew Foster, who founded the first school for the deaf in West Africa.

name: Ghanaian Sign Language
description: ASL-derived sign language introduced by Andrew Foster.

name: Kenyan Sign Language (KSL)
description: Sign language of Kenya, partially ASL-influenced.

name: Ugandan Sign Language
description: Sign language of Uganda; ASL-influenced; constitutionally recognized (1995).

name: Tanzanian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Tanzania; ASL-influenced.

name: Quebec Sign Language (LSQ)
description: French Sign Language descendant heavily influenced by ASL; distinct from both.

name: Brazilian Sign Language (Libras)
description: Sign language of Brazil; descended from LSF via E. Huet's founding of the Imperial Institute in 1857; legally recognized in Brazil since 2002.

name: Mexican Sign Language (LSM)
description: Sign language of Mexico; descended from LSF via Eduardo Huet.

name: Spanish Sign Language (LSE)
description: Sign language of Spain; LSF-influenced (Catalan SL is separate). Legally recognized 2007.

name: Catalan Sign Language (LSC)
description: Sign language of Catalonia, recognized as distinct from LSE.

name: Italian Sign Language (LIS)
description: Sign language of Italy.

name: Romanian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Romania.

name: Flemish Sign Language (VGT)
description: Sign language of Flemish Belgium; LSF-influenced via Belgian Sign Language.

name: French Belgian Sign Language (LSFB)
description: Sign language of French-speaking Belgium; close to LSF.

name: Sign Language of the Netherlands (NGT)
description: Sign language of the Netherlands; LSF-influenced (via French teachers at deaf schools).

name: Irish Sign Language (ISL)
description: Sign language of Ireland; LSF-derived; historically had gender-segregated varieties due to single-sex deaf schools.

name: Austrian Sign Language (ÖGS)
description: Sign language of Austria; some French Sign and German Sign influence; constitutionally recognized 2005.

name: Australian Sign Language (Auslan)
description: Sign language of Australia; descended from BSL via 19th-c. British deaf migrants and teachers.

name: New Zealand Sign Language (NZSL)
description: Sign language of New Zealand; BSL-derived; co-official language of NZ since 2006.

name: South African Sign Language (SASL)
description: Sign language of South Africa; BSL- and Irish SL-influenced; constitutionally recognized 2023 (12th official language).

name: Northern Ireland Sign Language
description: Sign language of Northern Ireland; closely related to BSL with some ISL influence due to Catholic-school history.

name: Maritime Sign Language (MSL)
description: Endangered sign language of the Canadian Maritimes; BSL-derived; in decline since the 1950s shift to ASL-based education.

name: German Sign Language (DGS)
description: Sign language of Germany; legally recognized 2002. Note: although the abbé de l'Épée's methods influenced German deaf education, DGS developed largely independently of LSF after Heinicke's oralist school in Leipzig.

name: Polish Sign Language (PJM)
description: Sign language of Poland; descended from DGS via the Warsaw deaf school (founded by Jakub Falkowski after training in Berlin and Vienna).

name: Czech Sign Language
description: Sign language of Czechia; German Sign-influenced; legally recognized 1998.

name: Slovak Sign Language
description: Sign language of Slovakia; closely related to Czech Sign.

name: Hungarian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Hungary; German Sign-influenced.

name: Israeli Sign Language (ISL)
description: Sign language of Israel; influenced by German Sign brought by Jewish deaf immigrants from Germany in the 1930s, plus contact with regional sign languages.

name: Swedish Sign Language (Svenskt teckenspråk)
description: Sign language of Sweden; Sweden was the first country to officially recognize a sign language as a minority language (1981).

name: Finnish Sign Language (FinSL)
description: Sign language of Finland; descended from Swedish Sign via Carl Oscar Malm, who brought it from Sweden in 1846; constitutionally recognized 1995.

name: Finland-Swedish Sign Language
description: Severely endangered sign language used by Swedish-speaking deaf Finns; sometimes classed as separate from FinSL.

name: Portuguese Sign Language (LGP)
description: Sign language of Portugal; introduced by Swedish deaf educator Pär Aron Borg; constitutionally recognized 1997.

name: Danish Sign Language
description: Sign language of Denmark; mixed historical influences (French, German); legally recognized 2014.

name: Norwegian Sign Language (NTS)
description: Sign language of Norway; closely related to Danish Sign due to shared Danish-rule deaf-education history.

name: Icelandic Sign Language (ÍTM)
description: Sign language of Iceland; closely related to Danish Sign; legally recognized as Iceland's first language of Deaf people in 2011.

name: Greenlandic Sign Language
description: Sign language of Greenland; Danish Sign-derived.

name: Faroese Sign Language
description: Sign language of the Faroe Islands; close to Danish Sign.

name: Russian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Russia; introduced via Pavlovsk and Saint Petersburg deaf schools; some Austrian/French Sign historical influence; spread across the USSR.

name: Ukrainian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Ukraine; historically closely related to Russian Sign; now diverging.

name: Belarusian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Belarus; closely related to Russian Sign.

name: Bulgarian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Bulgaria; Russian Sign-influenced via Soviet-era educational links.

name: Mongolian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Mongolia; Russian Sign-influenced via Soviet-era educational links.

name: Chinese Sign Language (CSL)
description: Sign language of mainland China; Shanghai and Beijing varieties recognized as distinct dialects. Some American Sign influence via 19th-c. missionary schools.

name: Hong Kong Sign Language
description: Sign language of Hong Kong; partly Shanghai SL-derived via 1948 deaf-school migration.

name: Taiwanese Sign Language (TSL)
description: Sign language of Taiwan; descended from Japanese Sign via the Japanese colonial period (1895–1945).

name: Korean Sign Language (KSL)
description: Sign language of South and North Korea; descended from Japanese Sign via the colonial period (1910–1945); legally recognized in South Korea 2016.

name: Thai Sign Language
description: Sign language of Thailand; ASL-influenced via Gallaudet-trained Thai teachers from 1951.

name: Vietnamese Sign Language
description: Sign language of Vietnam; three regional varieties (Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Haiphong) with substantial divergence; some French Sign influence via colonial schools.

name: Indo-Pakistani Sign Language (IPSL)
description: Sign language of the Indian subcontinent, used across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and parts of Nepal; substantially uniform despite political borders; among the largest sign-language communities in the world.

name: Nepali Sign Language
description: Sign language of Nepal; mostly independent of IPSL despite geographic overlap.

name: Saudi Sign Language
description: Sign language of Saudi Arabia; pan-Arab sign-language unification movements have not produced a single shared variety.

name: Egyptian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Egypt; the largest Arabic-speaking deaf community's sign language.

name: Jordanian Sign Language (LIU)
description: Sign language of Jordan.

name: Lebanese Sign Language
description: Sign language of Lebanon.

name: Kuwaiti Sign Language
description: Sign language of Kuwait.

name: Iranian Sign Language
description: Sign language of Iran; not part of Arab Sign family; classification debated.

name: Turkish Sign Language (TİD)
description: Sign language of Turkey; an Ottoman court sign tradition is documented but its relationship to modern TİD is debated.

name: Nicaraguan Sign Language (ISN)
description: Documented case of de novo language emergence: arose after 1977/1980 when deaf children were brought together in Managua schools without a shared signed input. Successive cohorts grammaticalized increasingly complex structures (case studies by Senghas, Kegl, Coppola).

name: Al-Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language (ABSL)
description: Village sign language used by deaf and hearing members of a single Bedouin community over three generations; emerged from a high incidence of hereditary deafness; studied by Sandler, Aronoff, Meir, Padden as a young-language case.

name: Kata Kolok (Bengkala Sign Language)
description: Village sign language used by deaf and hearing residents of Bengkala, where hereditary deafness has persisted for ~5+ generations. Studied by Marsaja and de Vos.

name: Adamorobe Sign Language (AdaSL)
description: Village sign language of Adamorobe; hereditary deafness present for centuries; documented by Nyst. Coexists with Ghanaian Sign Language.

name: Yucatec Maya Sign Language (Chican Sign)
description: Village sign language used by deaf and hearing Maya residents.

name: Ban Khor Sign Language
description: Village sign language of a rice-farming community in northeastern Thailand.

name: Alipur Sign Language
description: Village sign language of Alipur, a community with high hereditary deafness due to consanguineous marriage patterns.

name: Inuit Sign Language (Inuit Uukturausingit)
description: Severely endangered sign language of deaf Inuit; independent of ASL and other national SLs.

name: Hawaii Sign Language (HSL)
description: Endangered sign language of Hawaii, separate in origin from ASL though now extensively borrowed-from; documented by Lanesman, Meir, Sandler, and Padden as a recently identified independent language.

name: Providence Island Sign Language
description: Village sign language of Providence Island in the western Caribbean; documented by Washabaugh in the 1980s.

name: Central Taurus Sign Language (Mardin Sign)
description: Family sign language used by deaf members of a single extended Mardin family across multiple generations; subject of work by Zeshan and Dikyuva.

name: Plains Indian Sign Language (PISL, Hand Talk)
description: Sign-language lingua franca used across the Great Plains for inter-tribal communication, trade, and oratory; predates European contact; still used in some Indigenous communities. Distinct from ASL.

name: International Sign
description: Contact variety used at international deaf gatherings (WFD congresses, Deaflympics). Not a full language; uses gestural strategies and shared core lexicon. Formerly called Gestuno.

name: Makaton
description: Manual signing system using BSL signs alongside speech and symbols; designed as a communication aid for people with communication and learning disabilities, not a natural language.

name: Monastic Sign Languages (Cistercian etc.)
description: Limited-lexicon sign systems used by silent monastic orders (Cistercians, Trappists, Benedictines). Not full languages; used for specific domains during silence-rule periods.

name: Cued Speech
description: Manual system supplementing lipreading with handshapes that disambiguate phonemes; not a natural sign language but a phonemic representation of spoken languages. Invented by R. Orin Cornett.

name: Signed Exact English (SEE)
description: Manually coded form of English using ASL signs in English word order with added markers for English morphology; not a natural sign language; used pedagogically.

name: Proto-Salishan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Salishan family (~23 languages); homeland likely along the lower Fraser/Salish Sea.

name: Halkomelem
description: Central Salish language with Upriver, Downriver, and Island dialects.

name: Lushootseed
description: Central Salish language; documented extensively by Vi Hilbert.

name: Squamish (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim)
region: Howe Sound and Squamish River, BC
description: Central Salish language.

name: Sechelt (Shashishalhem)
description: Central Salish language.

name: Nuxalk (Bella Coola)
description: Salishan language geographically isolated from other Salishan; notable for extremely long consonant clusters (e.g., xłp̓x̣ʷłtłpłłskʷc̓).

name: St'át'imcets (Lillooet)
description: Interior Salish language.

name: Nlaka'pamux (Thompson)
description: Interior Salish language.

name: Secwepemctsín (Shuswap)
description: Interior Salish language.

name: Nsyilxcən (Okanagan-Colville)
description: Interior Salish language.

name: Snchitsu'umshtsn (Coeur d'Alene)
description: Interior Salish language.

name: Salish-Pend d'Oreille (Kalispel-Flathead)
description: Interior Salish language cluster including Flathead, Kalispel, and Spokane.

name: Klallam (Nəxʷsƛ̕áy̕əmúcən)
description: Central Salish language.

name: Tillamook
description: Salishan language; only Salishan outlier south of the Columbia; extinct.

name: Proto-Wakashan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Wakashan family; ~7 languages on Vancouver Island and adjacent BC mainland.

name: Kwak'wala (Kwakiutl)
region: Northern Vancouver Island and adjacent mainland
description: Northern Wakashan language; ethnographic documentation by Franz Boas.

name: Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka)
description: Southern Wakashan language; first Pacific Northwest language documented by Europeans (Cook's expedition 1778); subject of Edward Sapir's foundational work.

name: Heiltsuk (Bella Bella)
description: Northern Wakashan language.

name: Haisla
description: Northern Wakashan language.

name: Oowekyala
description: Northern Wakashan language closely related to Heiltsuk.

name: Ditidaht (Nitinaht)
description: Southern Wakashan language.

name: Makah
description: Southern Wakashan language; sole Wakashan language in the U.S.

name: Proto-Tsimshianic
region: Northern coast of BC and SE Alaska
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tsimshianic family (~4 languages).

name: Coast Tsimshian (Sm'álgyax)
description: Maritime Tsimshianic language.

name: Nisga'a
description: Tsimshianic language; subject of landmark Nisga'a Treaty (2000).

name: Gitxsan (Gitksan)
description: Tsimshianic language closely related to Nisga'a.

name: Southern Tsimshian (Sgüüxs)
description: Severely endangered Tsimshianic language.

name: Proto-Chimakuan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the small Chimakuan family (2 languages).

name: Quileute
description: Chimakuan language; last fluent first-language speakers passed in the 1990s.

name: Chemakum
description: Extinct Chimakuan language.

name: Proto-Muskogean
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Muskogean family of the U.S. Southeast.

name: Choctaw
region: Mississippi, Oklahoma; historically also LA, AL
description: Western Muskogean language; one of the larger surviving Southeastern Native languages.

name: Chickasaw
description: Western Muskogean language closely related to Choctaw.

name: Muscogee (Creek)
description: Eastern Muskogean language; lingua franca of the Creek Confederacy.

name: Seminole
description: Variety of Muscogee used by the Seminole; closely related to Muscogee-Creek proper.

name: Mikasuki (Miccosukee)
description: Eastern Muskogean language; one of two Seminole languages of Florida.

name: Alabama
description: Eastern Muskogean language; Alabama-Coushatta reservation in Texas.

name: Koasati (Coushatta)
description: Eastern Muskogean language closely related to Alabama.

name: Hitchiti
description: Extinct Eastern Muskogean language closely related to Mikasuki.

name: Apalachee
description: Extinct Eastern Muskogean language; speakers decimated in Queen Anne's War.

name: Proto-Caddoan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Caddoan family.

name: Caddo
description: Southern Caddoan language.

name: Pawnee
description: Northern Caddoan language.

name: Arikara
description: Northern Caddoan language closely related to Pawnee.

name: Wichita
description: Northern Caddoan language; last fluent native speaker died 2016.

name: Kitsai
description: Extinct Northern Caddoan language.

name: Proto-Kiowa-Tanoan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kiowa-Tanoan family; geographic separation between Kiowa (Plains) and Tanoan (Pueblo) reflects later Kiowa migration.

name: Kiowa
description: Plains language of the Kiowa; once-distant relative to Pueblo Tanoan languages confirmed by Whorf and Trager.

name: Tewa
region: Rio Grande Pueblos, New Mexico; also Arizona (Hopi-Tewa)
description: Tanoan language of six Pueblos plus Arizona Hopi-Tewa.

name: Northern Tiwa (Taos-Picuris)
region: Taos and Picuris Pueblos, New Mexico
description: Northern Tanoan variety.

name: Southern Tiwa (Sandia-Isleta)
region: Sandia and Isleta Pueblos, New Mexico
description: Southern Tanoan variety.

name: Towa (Jemez)
description: Tanoan language of Jemez Pueblo; sole surviving Towa variety.

name: Piro
description: Extinct Tanoan language.

name: Proto-Yuman-Cochimí
region: Lower Colorado River basin and Baja California
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Yuman-Cochimí family.

name: Mojave (Pipa Aha Macav)
description: River Yuman language.

name: Quechan (Yuma)
description: River Yuman language; namesake of the family.

name: Maricopa (Piipaash)
description: River Yuman language.

name: Havasupai-Hualapai (Upland Yuman)
description: Upland Pai branch Yuman language; dialect cluster including Havasupai, Hualapai, and Yavapai.

name: Yavapai
description: Pai-branch Yuman language.

name: Kumeyaay (Diegueño)
region: San Diego County, CA; northern Baja California
description: Delta-California Yuman language cluster including Kumeyaay, Ipai, and Tipai.

name: Cocopah (Kwapa)
description: Delta-California Yuman language.

name: Kiliwa
description: Most divergent Yuman language; sister to all others.

name: Paipai
description: Pai-branch Yuman language.

name: Cochimí
description: Extinct Cochimí language; documented by 17th–18th c. Spanish missionaries.

name: Proto-Pomoan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Pomoan family (7 languages).

name: Eastern Pomo
description: Pomoan language.

name: Northern Pomo
description: Pomoan language.

name: Central Pomo
description: Pomoan language.

name: Southern Pomo
description: Pomoan language.

name: Southeastern Pomo
description: Pomoan language.

name: Kashaya
description: Pomoan language.

name: Northeastern Pomo
description: Extinct Pomoan language.

name: Proto-Chumashan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Chumashan family; all daughters extinct/dormant.

name: Barbareño Chumash
description: Dormant Chumashan language; last speaker Mary Yee died 1965; revitalization underway.

name: Ineseño Chumash
description: Dormant Chumashan language.

name: Ventureño Chumash
description: Dormant Chumashan language.

name: Obispeño Chumash
description: Most divergent Chumashan language; dormant.

name: Purisimeño Chumash
description: Extinct Chumashan language.

name: Island Chumash (Cruzeño)
description: Extinct Chumashan language of Santa Cruz and Santa Rosa Islands.

name: Proto-Yokutsan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Yokutsan family.

name: Yowlumne (Yawelmani)
description: Yokutsan language; canonical example in generative phonology (Kisseberth, Newman).

name: Chukchansi
description: Yokutsan language.

name: Tachi
description: Yokutsan language.

name: Proto-Sahaptian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Sahaptian family (Sahaptin and Nez Perce).

name: Sahaptin (Ichishkíin)
description: Sahaptian language cluster including Yakama, Umatilla, Walla Walla, Palouse.

name: Nez Perce (Nimipuutímt)
description: Sahaptian language.

name: Klamath-Modoc
description: Language of the Klamath and Modoc peoples; sometimes grouped with Sahaptian under Plateau Penutian. Now severely endangered.

name: Proto-Wintuan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Wintuan family.

name: Wintu
description: Wintuan language.

name: Nomlaki
description: Wintuan language.

name: Patwin
description: Wintuan language.

name: Proto-Maiduan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Maiduan family.

name: Maidu (Northeastern)
description: Maiduan language.

name: Nisenan
description: Maiduan language.

name: Konkow (Concow)
description: Maiduan language.

name: Proto-Utian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Utian family (Miwok and Costanoan).

name: Ohlone (Costanoan)
region: San Francisco Bay Area to Monterey, CA
description: Costanoan language cluster; revitalization efforts underway.

name: Coast Miwok
description: Miwok language.

name: Lake Miwok

name: Soninke (Sarakolé)
description: Northwestern Mande language; language of the Ghana Empire (Wagadu) of the 8th–13th c.

name: Bozo
description: Northwestern Mande language cluster; speakers historically associated with Niger River fishing.

name: Dyula (Jula)
description: Manding-cluster Mande language; major lingua franca of West African trade routes since the medieval period.

name: Maninka (Malinké)
description: Manding-cluster Mande language; language of the historical Mali Empire (Mansa Musa).

name: Bisa (Busa)
description: Eastern Mande language.

name: Dan (Gio/Yacouba)
description: Southeastern Mande language.

name: Mano
description: Southeastern Mande language closely related to Dan.

name: Guro
description: Southern Mande language.

name: Samogo
description: Northwestern Mande language cluster.

name: Bobo (Bobo Madaré)
description: Northwestern Mande language.

name: Serer (Sereer-Siin)
description: Senegambian Atlantic language; speakers historically resisted Islamization until the 19th c.

name: Jola (Diola)
description: Bak-branch Atlantic language cluster of Casamance.

name: Balanta
description: Bak-branch Atlantic language; largest indigenous language of Guinea-Bissau.

name: Mankanya
description: Bak-branch Atlantic language.

name: Manjak
description: Bak-branch Atlantic language.

name: Pepel (Papel)
description: Bak-branch Atlantic language.

name: Temne
description: Mel-branch Atlantic language; one of the two largest languages of Sierra Leone alongside Mende.

name: Limba
description: Mel-branch Atlantic language.

name: Kissi
description: Mel-branch Atlantic language.

name: Bullom (Sherbro-Bullom)
description: Mel-branch Atlantic language cluster.

name: Bijago
description: Atlantic language; divergent from rest of Atlantic and sometimes treated as separate branch.

name: Nalu
description: Atlantic language; branch position debated.

name: Mòoré (Mossi)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language; largest language of Burkina Faso; language of the historical Mossi kingdoms.

name: Dagbani (Dagbanli)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language; lingua franca of northern Ghana.

name: Frafra (Gurene)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language.

name: Mampruli
description: Oti-Volta Gur language closely related to Dagbani.

name: Kusaal
description: Oti-Volta Gur language.

name: Likpakpaln (Konkomba)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language.

name: Dagaare (Dagara)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language.

name: Gurma (Gourmanché)
description: Oti-Volta Gur language.

name: Kabiye
description: Gur language; one of two national languages of Togo (with Ewe).

name: Supyire (Senufo)
description: Senufo branch language. Senufo's place inside Gur is debated; some recent classifications treat Senufo as a separate Niger-Congo branch.

name: Cebaara (Senufo)
description: Senufo branch language.

name: Bwamu
description: Gur language.

name: Lobiri (Lobi)
description: Gur language.

name: Ga
description: Ga-Dangme Kwa language; language of the Greater Accra region.

name: Dangme (Adangme)
description: Ga-Dangme Kwa language closely related to Ga.

name: Anyi (Agni)
description: Tano-branch Kwa language closely related to Akan/Twi.

name: Baoulé (Baule)
description: Tano-branch Kwa language; major language of Côte d'Ivoire.

name: Nzema
description: Tano-branch Kwa language.

name: Fon (Fongbe)
description: Gbe Kwa language; language of the historical Kingdom of Dahomey; ritual language of Vodun.

name: Gun (Gungbe)
description: Gbe Kwa language closely related to Fon.

name: Aja
description: Gbe Kwa language.

name: Guang
description: Guang-branch Kwa language cluster.

name: Edo (Bini)
description: Edoid Volta-Niger language; language of the historical Benin Empire (kingdom).

name: Urhobo
description: Edoid Volta-Niger language.

name: Isoko
description: Edoid Volta-Niger language closely related to Urhobo.

name: Esan (Ishan)
description: Edoid Volta-Niger language.

name: Igala
description: Yoruboid Volta-Niger language; language of the historical Igala Kingdom.

name: Itsekiri
description: Yoruboid Volta-Niger language; closely related to Yoruba despite geographic separation.

name: Ebira
description: Nupoid Volta-Niger language.

name: Nupe
description: Nupoid Volta-Niger language; language of the historical Nupe Kingdom.

name: Gbagyi (Gwari)
description: Nupoid Volta-Niger language.

name: Idoma
description: Idomoid Volta-Niger language.

name: Alago
description: Idomoid Volta-Niger language closely related to Idoma.

name: Efik
description: Lower Cross River language; lingua franca of the historical Calabar trading state; prestigious 19th-c. literary language.

name: Ibibio
description: Lower Cross River language closely related to Efik; speakers more numerous.

name: Anaang (Annang)
description: Lower Cross River language.

name: Ekoid (Ejagham)
description: Bendi Cross River language cluster; speakers historically used the Nsibidi ideographic writing system.

name: Oron
description: Lower Cross River language.

name: Kana (Ogoni)
description: Ogoni Cross River language.

name: Zande (Pazande)
region: DRC, South Sudan, Central African Republic
description: Ubangian language; subject of Evans-Pritchard's classic ethnography of witchcraft and oracles.

name: Ngbandi
description: Ubangian language; source/base of Sango (creolized form).

name: Sango
description: Creolized form of Ngbandi developed as lingua franca along the Ubangi River during the colonial period; national language of CAR.

name: Gbaya
description: Ubangian language cluster.

name: Banda
description: Ubangian language cluster.

name: Ngbaka
description: Ubangian language.

name: Mumuye
description: Adamawa language; speakers known for distinctive sculptural tradition.

name: Mbum
description: Adamawa language cluster.

name: Longuda
description: Adamawa language.

name: Bassa
description: Kru language; historically written in the indigenous Bassa Vah script (early 20th c., Thomas Flo Lewis).

name: Klao (Kru)
description: Kru language; namesake of the family.

name: Grebo
description: Kru language.

name: Krahn (Wee)
description: Kru language.

name: Bété
description: Kru language cluster of central-western Côte d'Ivoire.

name: Dida
description: Kru language.

name: Godié
description: Kru language.

name: Izon (Central Ijaw)
description: Largest Ijoid language.

name: Kalabari
description: Eastern Ijoid language.

name: Nembe
description: Eastern Ijoid language.

name: Okrika
description: Eastern Ijoid language.

name: Defaka
description: Critically endangered Ijoid language; sometimes treated as separate branch within Ijoid.

name: Tomo Kan Dogon
description: Dogon language; cluster includes ~20 mutually unintelligible varieties.

name: Jamsay Dogon
description: Dogon language; large speaker population among the Dogon group.

name: Toro So Dogon
description: Dogon language; basis of the standard 'Dogon' literary form (Toro Tegu).

name: Bangime
description: Isolate spoken by people who self-identify as Dogon but speak a language unrelated to Dogon or to any other family. Documented by Heath, Hantgan.

name: Berom (Birom)
description: Plateau (Platoid) Benue-Congo language.

name: Tarok
description: Plateau Benue-Congo language.

name: Eggon
description: Plateau Benue-Congo language.

name: Kambari
description: Kainji Benue-Congo language.

name: Reshe
description: Kainji Benue-Congo language.

name: Jukun
description: Jukunoid Benue-Congo language; language of the historical Kwararafa confederation.

name: Tiv
description: Tivoid Benue-Congo language; largest Benue-Congo language outside the Bantoid-Bantu group.

name: Heiban (Otoro)
description: Heiban-branch Kordofanian Niger-Congo language.

name: Talodi
description: Talodi-branch Kordofanian Niger-Congo language.

name: Rashad
description: Rashad-branch Kordofanian Niger-Congo language.

name: Katla
description: Katla-branch Kordofanian Niger-Congo language.

name: Proto-Tibeto-Burman
description: Reconstructed ancestor of all non-Sinitic Sino-Tibetan languages in the classical (Matisoff/STEDT) view. Whether 'Tibeto-Burman' constitutes a valid clade is disputed: Sino-Bodic and other proposals reject a primary Sinitic vs. TB split, treating Sinitic as one branch among many. Used here as a convenience node grouping non-Sinitic ST branches.

name: Proto-Lolo-Burmese
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Lolo-Burmese (Burmic, Ngwi-Burmese) subgroup, comprising the Burmish branch (Burmese and relatives) and the Loloish/Ngwi branch (Yi, Lisu, Lahu, Akha, etc.). Subgroup is one of the most securely established within Tibeto-Burman.

name: Proto-Burmish
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Burmish branch of Lolo-Burmese, including Burmese, Achang, Zaiwa, Maru, and Lashi.

name: Proto-Loloish (Ngwi)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Loloish/Ngwi branch of Lolo-Burmese. Bradley's classification subdivides it into Northern (Yi/Nuosu), Central (Lisu, Lahu), Southern (Akha, Hani), and Southeastern groups. Has wide diversity across southwestern China and northern Southeast Asia.

name: Proto-Bodish
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Bodish subgroup, including the Tibetic languages (descended from Old Tibetan) and the West Bodish/East Bodish languages of Bhutan, Nepal, and adjacent regions. Bodish itself is sometimes grouped with Tshangla and other languages in a wider 'Bodish' or 'Tibeto-Kanauri' subgroup.

name: Proto-Tibetic (Old Tibetan)
description: The ancestor of all modern Tibetic languages, attested in Old Tibetan inscriptions (c. 7th–9th c.) and early Dunhuang manuscripts. Classical Tibetan is its codified literary continuation. Modern Tibetic languages (Central, Khams, Amdo, Ladakhi, Balti, Dzongkha, Sherpa) descend from Old Tibetan, though some divergences predate the literary standard.

name: Proto-Qiangic
region: Sichuan and adjacent regions of southwestern China
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Qiangic subgroup of Tibeto-Burman, encompassing Qiang, Pumi, Muya, Queyu, rGyalrong (sometimes treated as separate), and historically Tangut. Internal subgrouping and external relations (Naic, rGyalrongic) are actively debated; some scholars treat rGyalrongic as a separate primary branch rather than a Qiangic subgroup.

name: Proto-Naic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Naic (Naish) languages — Naxi, Na (Mosuo), and Laze. Often grouped with Qiangic in older classifications, but increasingly treated as a separate Sino-Tibetan branch with possible affinities to Lolo-Burmese.

name: Proto-Tani
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tani (Mirish/Abor-Miri-Dafla) languages of central Arunachal Pradesh and adjacent areas. Includes Western Tani (Apatani, Nyishi) and Eastern Tani (Adi, Galo, Mising, Tagin).

name: Proto-Kuki-Chin (Proto-Kukish)
region: Western Myanmar, Mizoram, Manipur, Chin Hills
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kuki-Chin (Kukish) branch, including Mizo, Hakha Chin, Falam Chin, Tedim, Thadou, Paite, and many others. Internal classification distinguishes Northern, Central, Maraic, and Southern Chin subgroups.

name: Proto-Bodo-Garo
region: Assam, Meghalaya, North Bengal, northern Bangladesh
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Bodo-Garo (Boro-Garo) branch, including Bodo, Garo, Tripuri (Kokborok), Dimasa, Rabha, and Tiwa. Often grouped with Konyak, Northern Naga, and Jingphoic into a 'Sal' or 'Bodo-Konyak-Jingpho' supergroup.

name: Proto-Konyak (Northern Naga)
region: Northeastern Nagaland and adjacent Arunachal Pradesh
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Konyak/Northern Naga subgroup, including Konyak, Phom, Chang, Khiamniungan, Wancho, and Nocte. Distinct from the broader 'Naga' cover term, which is geographic rather than genetic and includes several unrelated Tibeto-Burman branches.

name: Proto-Jingphoic
region: Northern Myanmar (Kachin State), Yunnan, northeastern India
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Jingphoic (Kachinic) languages, principally Jingpho/Kachin and the related Singpho varieties.

name: Proto-Kiranti
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kiranti (Rai) languages of eastern Nepal, including Limbu, Bantawa, Chamling, Khaling, Thulung, and many others. Kiranti is one of the most morphologically conservative Tibeto-Burman subgroups, retaining complex verbal agreement.

name: Proto-Tamangic (TGTM)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tamangic (Tamang-Gurung-Thakali-Manangba, 'TGTM') languages of Nepal. Usually classified within wider Bodish.

name: Proto-Karbic (Mikir)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Karbic (Mikir) languages spoken in central Assam. Position within Tibeto-Burman is debated; sometimes grouped with Kuki-Chin or treated as an independent branch.

name: Tangut (西夏文)
region: Western Xia (modern Ningxia, Gansu, eastern Xinjiang)
description: Extinct language of the Western Xia (Xi Xia) empire (1038–1227 CE), recorded in a logographic script of c. 6,000 characters commissioned in 1036. Deciphered progressively from the early 20th century after the Khara-Khoto manuscripts were found. Classification as Qiangic is the majority view (Jacques, Gong); some (Beckwith) treat it as more remote.

name: Qiang
description: Northern and Southern Qiang are mutually unintelligible and sometimes treated as separate languages. Spoken by the Qiang ethnic group (recognized as one of China's 55 minorities). Northern Qiang is non-tonal; Southern Qiang is tonal.

name: Pumi (Prinmi)
description: Closely related to Qiang and Muya. Northern and Southern varieties; speakers (the Pumi nationality in China and Prinmi in adjacent Tibet) are largely Tibetan Buddhists.

name: Naxi (Nakhi)
description: Language of the Naxi people, traditionally written in the Dongba pictographic script — the only living pictographic script in use, employed primarily for Dongba religious texts. A separate syllabic script (Geba) also exists.

name: Yi (Nuosu / Northern Yi)
description: Cover term for several related but often mutually unintelligible Loloish languages spoken by the Yi nationality of China; Nuosu (Northern Yi) is the largest and is the basis for the standard literary form. Written in the Yi syllabary (Cuan or modern standardized 'Liangshan Yi') of c. 800 standardized characters since 1980.

name: Lisu
region: Yunnan, northern Myanmar, Thailand, northeastern India
description: Central Loloish language; written in the Fraser script (developed c. 1915 by missionary Sara Ba Thaw with James O. Fraser), a rotated-Latin alphabet, and more recently also in a Pollard-derived script and pinyin-style romanization.

name: Lahu
description: Central Loloish language with several mutually intelligible dialects (Lahu Na, Lahu Shi, Lahu Nyi). Written in a Latin-based orthography developed by missionaries.

name: Akha
region: Yunnan, eastern Myanmar (Shan State), northern Thailand, Laos
description: Southern Loloish language closely related to Hani. Multiple competing orthographies (missionary, Chinese, Thai-based) reflect the cross-border distribution of the Akha people.

name: Hani
region: Southern Yunnan and adjacent Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar
description: Southern Loloish language closely related to Akha. Official Hani romanization developed in 1957. The Hani are recognized as one of China's 55 minority nationalities.

name: Old Burmese
description: Earliest attested stage of Burmese, recorded in the Myazedi inscription (1113 CE, Pagan), a quadrilingual text in Burmese, Pyu, Mon, and Pali. The Burmese script is derived from the Mon script, itself ultimately from Brahmi via Pallava.

name: Middle Burmese
region: Central and Upper Myanmar (Toungoo and early Konbaung)
description: Intermediate stage between Old and Modern Burmese, marked by major phonological changes including the loss of medial -l- and shifts in tone system.

name: Achang (Ngochang)
region: Western Yunnan and northern Myanmar (Kachin State)
description: Closest extant relative of Burmese alongside Zaiwa and Maru. Recognized as one of the official ethnic groups in both China and Myanmar.

name: Zaiwa (Atsi)
description: Burmish language closely related to Burmese; speakers are often classified as part of the Jingpo/Kachin ethnic group despite linguistic distinctness.

name: Pyu
region: Central Myanmar (Pyu city-states: Sri Ksetra, Beikthano, Halin)
description: Extinct Sino-Tibetan language of the Pyu city-states of central Myanmar (c. 2nd c. BCE–9th c. CE), attested in inscriptions in a Brahmi-derived script and most importantly in the quadrilingual Myazedi inscription (1113 CE). Its position within Tibeto-Burman is unresolved; Beckwith argues for an isolate position, others link it to Burmish or Sal.

name: S'gaw Karen
region: Myanmar (Kayin State, Irrawaddy Delta), western Thailand
description: Largest Karenic language by speakers (c. 1.5–2 million). Written in a Mon-derived Karen script developed by American Baptist missionary Jonathan Wade (c. 1830). The S'gaw are the demographic majority among Karen peoples in Myanmar.

name: Pwo Karen
region: Myanmar (Kayin State, Mon State, delta), western Thailand
description: Second-largest Karenic language; comprises Eastern, Western, Northern, and Phrae Pwo varieties, sometimes treated as separate languages. Written in a separate Pwo Karen script derived from Mon, distinct from but related to the S'gaw Karen script.

name: Kayah (Karenni / Red Karen)
region: Kayah State, eastern Myanmar; refugee communities in Thailand
description: Central Karenic language of the Kayah (Karenni) people; Eastern and Western dialects. Written in the Kayah Li script, developed c. 1962 by Htae Bu Phae.

name: Kayan (Padaung)
region: Kayah State and southern Shan State, Myanmar
description: Central Karenic language; the Padaung subgroup is internationally known for the brass neck rings traditionally worn by women.

name: Amdo Tibetan
description: Major Tibetic variety; non-tonal (in contrast to Central and Khams Tibetan), preserving certain conservative phonological features. Written form uses Classical Tibetan orthography.

name: Khams Tibetan
region: Kham region (western Sichuan, eastern Tibet AR, northwestern Yunnan, southern Qinghai)
description: Major Tibetic variety; tonal, with multiple dialect clusters. Speakers traditionally identify as Khampa.

name: Ladakhi
description: Western Archaic Tibetic language; phonologically conservative (preserves consonant clusters lost in Central Tibetan). Written in the Tibetan script; speakers are predominantly Tibetan Buddhist.

name: Balti
description: Western Archaic Tibetic language; like Ladakhi, preserves Old Tibetan consonant clusters. Speakers are predominantly Shia Muslim, distinguishing Balti culturally from most other Tibetic-speaking groups. Has been written historically in both Tibetan and Perso-Arabic (Balti-Persian) scripts.

name: Sherpa
description: Tibetic language of the Sherpa people, who migrated from Kham (eastern Tibet) to the Nepali Himalayas in the 15th–16th centuries. Traditionally written in Tibetan script; Devanagari also used in Nepal.

name: Sikkimese (Drenjongke)
description: Tibetic language closely related to Dzongkha and Sherpa, spoken by the Bhutia community of Sikkim. Written in Tibetan script.

name: Tshangla (Sharchopkha)
region: Eastern Bhutan, southeastern Tibet AR, and Arunachal Pradesh
description: Major language of eastern Bhutan; the most widely spoken non-Dzongkha language in the country. Sometimes classified as East Bodish, sometimes as a separate Bodish branch closely related to but distinct from Tibetic.

name: Limbu (Yakthung)
description: Major Kiranti language. Written in the Limbu (Sirijanga) script, traditionally attributed to King Sirijunga Hang in the 9th century, revived in the 18th century by Sirijunga Xin Thebe. Devanagari also used.

name: Bantawa
description: Most widely spoken Central Kiranti language. Like other Kiranti languages, preserves polypersonal verbal agreement.

name: Chamling (Rodung)
description: Central Kiranti language closely related to Bantawa.

name: Khaling
description: Western Kiranti language documented in detail by Jacques and colleagues; notable for complex morphophonology.

name: Thulung
description: Western Kiranti language; classification within Kiranti debated, sometimes treated as a primary branch.

name: Tamang
description: Largest Tamangic language; multiple regional varieties (Eastern and Western Tamang sometimes treated as separate languages). Traditionally written in Devanagari; the Tamyig script is a more recent indigenous development.

name: Gurung (Tamu Kyi)
region: Central Nepal (Gandaki, especially Lamjung, Kaski, Manang)
description: Tamangic language of the Gurung people, who have historically been heavily represented in the British and Indian Gurkha regiments.

name: Thakali
description: Tamangic language with several local varieties; speakers are traditionally traders along the Kali Gandaki valley salt route between Tibet and India.

name: Manangba (Nyeshangte)
description: Tamangic language of the Nyeshang valley; speakers historically engaged in long-distance trade across Asia.

name: Apatani (Tanw)
region: Ziro Valley, Lower Subansiri, Arunachal Pradesh
description: Western Tani language with a distinctive system of tone and nasal vowels; spoken by the Apatani, known for terraced wet-rice cultivation in the Ziro Valley.

name: Nyishi (Nishi)
description: Most widely spoken Western Tani language; the Nyishi are the largest single ethnic group in Arunachal Pradesh.

name: Adi
region: East Siang, Upper Siang, West Siang, Arunachal Pradesh
description: Eastern Tani language cluster (Padam, Minyong, Pasi, Bori, Karko, etc., sometimes treated as separate languages). 'Adi' was formerly known as 'Abor'.

name: Galo
region: West Siang and Lepa Rada, Arunachal Pradesh
description: Western/Eastern Tani transitional language closely related to Adi.

name: Mising (Plains Miri)
description: Eastern Tani language of the Mising, descended from Adi speakers who migrated to the plains of Assam centuries ago. Heavy contact with Assamese has produced significant lexical and structural influence.

name: Tagin
description: Western Tani language related to Nyishi.

name: Mizo (Lushai)
region: Mizoram (India), Chin State (Myanmar), Chittagong Hill Tracts (Bangladesh)
description: Central Kuki-Chin language; official language of Mizoram. Written in a Latin-based orthography developed by Welsh missionaries James Herbert Lorrain and Frederick William Savidge in 1894. Has served as a lingua franca across the Kuki-Chin region.

name: Hakha Chin (Lai)
region: Chin State, Myanmar; diaspora in the US (notably Indianapolis)
description: Central Kuki-Chin language; the official language of Chin State and the Chin diaspora's most widely used variety.

name: Falam Chin
description: Central Kuki-Chin language closely related to Hakha; also called Laizo.

name: Tedim (Tiddim Chin)
region: Northern Chin State, Myanmar; Manipur, India
description: Northern Kuki-Chin language; major lingua franca of northern Chin Hills.

name: Thadou (Kuki)
description: Northern Kuki-Chin language; the most widely spoken of the languages identifying as 'Kuki' in northeast India.

name: Paite
description: Northern Kuki-Chin language closely related to Tedim and Thadou.

name: Bodo (Boro)
description: Largest Bodo-Garo language; a Scheduled Language of India and co-official language of Assam. Written in Devanagari since 1963 (previously Latin and Assamese script have been used).

name: Garo (A·chik)
description: Major Bodo-Garo language; written in Latin (developed by American Baptist missionaries) and Bengali scripts. The Garo are a matrilineal society.

name: Tripuri (Kokborok)
description: Major Bodo-Garo language and a co-official language of Tripura. 'Kokborok' (literally 'language of the Bodos/people') is the autonym. Written in both Latin and Bengali scripts; choice of script is politically contested.

name: Dimasa
description: Bodo-Garo language of the Dimasa Kachari, whose Dimasa Kingdom (Kachari Kingdom) was a significant pre-colonial polity in the Brahmaputra Valley.

name: Rabha
description: Bodo-Garo language; severely endangered with most speakers shifting to Assamese.

name: Konyak
region: Mon district (Nagaland) and adjacent Arunachal Pradesh
description: Major Northern Naga language; the Konyak are the largest Naga group in Nagaland and historically known for headhunting practices that persisted into the mid-20th century.

name: Phom
description: Northern Naga language closely related to Konyak and Chang.

name: Chang
description: Northern Naga language.

name: Wancho
description: Northern Naga language; the Wancho script was developed in 2001 by Banwang Losu and added to Unicode 13.0 (2020).

name: Nocte
description: Northern Naga language closely related to Wancho.

name: Ao
description: Central Naga language of the Ao Naga, the first Naga group to convert to Christianity (1872). Two main dialects, Chungli and Mongsen, with the former serving as the literary standard. 'Naga' is not a linguistic clade; Ao belongs to the Central Naga subgroup, distinct from Konyak/Northern Naga and Angami-Pochuri.

name: Angami (Tenyidie)
description: Major Angami-Pochuri language; Tenyidie is the literary form. Functions as a lingua franca in southern Nagaland.

name: Sema (Sumi)
description: Major Angami-Pochuri Naga language.

name: Lotha
description: Central Naga language closely related to Ao.

name: Jingpho (Kachin)
description: Principal Jingphoic language; the literary and political language of the Kachin people. Written in a Latin-based orthography developed in the 1890s by American Baptist missionary Ola Hanson. Functions as a lingua franca among the various ethnic groups making up the Kachin coalition.

name: Karbi (Mikir)
description: Principal Karbic language; an associate official language of Assam. Written in Latin script (and historically also Assamese script).

name: Lepcha (Róng)
region: Sikkim, Darjeeling, southwestern Bhutan, eastern Nepal
description: Indigenous language of Sikkim and the Lepcha people. Written in the Lepcha script (Róng script), developed c. 1700 traditionally attributed to King Chakdor Namgyal or scholar Thikúng Mensalóng. Position within Sino-Tibetan disputed: variously grouped with Mahakiranti, with Bodish, or treated as an independent branch.

name: Old Egyptian
region: Ancient Egypt (Old Kingdom and First Intermediate Period)
description: Earliest fully-attested stage of Egyptian; the language of the Pyramid Texts (Old Kingdom royal tomb inscriptions, c. 2400–2300 BCE) and Old Kingdom autobiographical inscriptions. Written in hieroglyphs and an early form of hieratic.

name: Middle Egyptian (Classical Egyptian)
approxDate: c. 2100–1700 BCE (spoken); used as literary language to c. 400 CE
description: Spoken form of the Middle Kingdom; subsequently became the 'classical' literary language of Egypt, used in monumental and religious inscriptions for nearly 2,000 years after it had ceased to be spoken (compare Latin in medieval Europe). The Coffin Texts, Story of Sinuhe, and most temple inscriptions of all later periods are in Middle Egyptian.

name: Late Egyptian
region: Ancient Egypt (late New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period)
description: Vernacular Egyptian of the late New Kingdom and after, used in administrative texts, letters, and Ramesside literary works (e.g. the Tale of Wenamun, the Two Brothers). Marked by analytic syntax replacing the synthetic features of Middle Egyptian, definite/indefinite article emergence, and increased Semitic loanwords from contact with the Levant.

name: Demotic Egyptian
region: Egypt (Late Period, Ptolemaic, and Roman Egypt)
description: Vernacular and chancery form of Egyptian in the Late, Ptolemaic, and Roman periods, written in the Demotic script — a cursive simplification of hieratic. The Demotic text on the Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) was central to Champollion's decipherment of the hieroglyphs. Coptic descends from Demotic.

name: Proto-Arabic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of all Arabic varieties, both literary (Classical) and spoken (Neo-Arabic). Diverged from a Northwest Semitic/Central Semitic ancestor; the precise sister relationships within Central Semitic (Arabic, Northwest Semitic, Old South Arabian) are debated.

name: Old Arabic
description: Pre-Islamic stage of Arabic, attested in inscriptions across the Arabian Peninsula and Levant in Safaitic, Hismaic, Dadanitic, Thamudic, and Nabataean scripts. The pre-Islamic poetic koine and the language of the Qur'an descend from Old Arabic. Modern scholarship (Al-Jallad) increasingly treats it as a continuum rather than one language.

name: Neo-Arabic (spoken Arabic continuum)
region: Arabic-speaking world (Maghreb to Mesopotamia, Sudan to Anatolia)
description: Cover node for the spoken Arabic dialect continuum. Modern dialects descend not from Classical Arabic but from spoken varieties that diverged from a common Old Arabic source through the Islamic conquests (7th–8th c. CE). The koineization producing the major groups (Maghrebi, Egyptian, Levantine, etc.) occurred in early Islamic cities.

name: Iraqi Arabic (Mesopotamian Arabic)
region: Iraq, southeastern Turkey (Anatolian Arabic), Khuzestan (Iran), eastern Syria
description: Mesopotamian Arabic dialect group; subdivided into qeltu dialects (Christian and Jewish Baghdadi, Mosul, Anatolian) and gilit dialects (Muslim Baghdadi, southern Iraqi, Khuzestani). The qeltu/gilit split reflects the medieval pre-Islamic vs. post-Bedouin migration layers. Significant Aramaic, Akkadian, Persian, and Turkish substrate/adstrate.

name: Yemeni Arabic
description: Highly conservative Arabic dialect group preserving features lost elsewhere (e.g. pre-Islamic /q/, productive internal passive). Major sub-varieties include San'ani, Ta'izzi-Adeni, Tihami, and Hadrami. Significant Old South Arabian substrate.

name: Hijazi Arabic
region: Western Saudi Arabia (Hijaz: Mecca, Medina, Jeddah)
description: Peninsular Arabic dialect of the western Arabian coastal region. Urban Hijazi (Mecca, Medina, Jeddah) is distinct from Bedouin Hijazi and serves as a regional prestige variety.

name: Najdi Arabic
region: Central Saudi Arabia (Najd: Riyadh, Qassim, Hail)
description: Peninsular Arabic dialect of the Najdi plateau; the basis of the prestige urban Saudi koine. Includes the Aniza, Shammar, and other tribal sub-varieties.

name: Sudanese Arabic
description: Sudanic Arabic dialect group; Khartoum/Omdurman Arabic is the prestige variety. Substantial Nubian and other African-language substrate, especially in lexicon for material culture.

name: Chadian Arabic (Shuwa Arabic)
region: Chad, northern Cameroon, northeastern Nigeria, western Sudan
description: Sudanic Arabic variety spoken by the Shuwa Arab populations across the Lake Chad basin. Functions as a major lingua franca of N'Djamena and the Sahel; not to be confused with the Chadic branch of Afroasiatic.

name: Hassaniya (Hassānīya)
region: Mauritania, Western Sahara, southern Morocco, northwestern Mali, Senegal River valley
description: Western Saharan Arabic, brought to the region by the Beni Hassan Arab tribes (13th–17th c.). Heavy Berber (Zenaga) substrate. The literary register, used in the Mauritanian tradition of moral poetry (gāf), is a prestige form.

name: Najrani Arabic
region: Najran region (southwestern Saudi Arabia) and adjacent Yemen
description: Conservative Peninsular Arabic dialect group of the Najran region, transitional between Yemeni and Najdi types.

name: Bahrani Arabic
region: Bahrain, eastern Saudi Arabia, Qatif, Hasa, Oman, Kuwait (among the Baharna community)
description: Peninsular Arabic dialect of the Baharna (Shia indigenous population of Bahrain and eastern Arabia). Preserves features of the pre-Islamic settled Arabic of eastern Arabia; distinct from the gilit/Bedouin dialects of the same region.

name: Omani Arabic
region: Oman, eastern UAE, formerly Zanzibar and the Swahili coast
description: Peninsular Arabic dialect of Oman; carried to the East African coast and Zanzibar during Omani imperial expansion (17th–19th c.). Oman's Dhofari and interior varieties retain particularly archaic features.

name: Old Aramaic
description: Earliest attested Aramaic, used in the inscriptions of the Aramean kingdoms (Sam'al, Aram-Damascus, Hamath, Bit-Adini). Written in a Phoenician-derived alphabet that became the ancestor of the Imperial Aramaic, square Hebrew, Syriac, Nabataean, Palmyrene, and ultimately Arabic scripts.

name: Imperial Aramaic (Achaemenid Aramaic)
region: Achaemenid Empire (from Egypt to the Indus)
description: Aramaic standardized as the chancery language of the Neo-Assyrian, Neo-Babylonian, and especially Achaemenid Persian empires. Texts include the Elephantine papyri and the Aramaic portions of Ezra and Daniel. The Imperial Aramaic script is ancestral to most West Asian alphabets including Hebrew square script, Syriac, and Nabataean→Arabic.

name: Middle Aramaic
region: Levant, Mesopotamia, northern Arabia, southeastern Anatolia
description: Post-Achaemenid stage marked by dialectal fragmentation into clearly regional varieties: Hasmonaean and Qumran Aramaic, Nabataean, Palmyrene, Hatran, Edessene (Old Syriac), and Jewish Palestinian Aramaic. Boundary with Late Aramaic conventionally placed around 200 CE.

name: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic
description: Eastern Late Aramaic dialect; the language of the Babylonian Talmud (compiled c. 500 CE) and the geonic responsa. Heavily influenced by Akkadian and Middle Persian. The literary tradition continued in Jewish religious use long after it ceased to be a spoken language.

name: Jewish Palestinian Aramaic (Galilean Aramaic)
description: Western Late Aramaic dialect; the language of the Jerusalem Talmud, the Palestinian Targums (e.g. Targum Neofiti), and most Aramaic inscriptions from late antique Palestine. Closely related to the Aramaic spoken by Jesus and his contemporaries.

name: Samaritan Aramaic
description: Western Late Aramaic dialect of the Samaritan community; the language of the Samaritan Targum and other Samaritan religious literature. Written in the Samaritan script (a direct descendant of Paleo-Hebrew, not the square Aramaic script).

name: Christian Palestinian Aramaic
region: Byzantine Palestine and Transjordan; Sinai monasteries
description: Western Late Aramaic dialect of Melkite Christian communities in Palestine; written in a distinctive variant of the Syriac Estrangela script. Used for biblical and liturgical translations from Greek; the spoken language was likely displaced by Arabic after the 8th c.

name: Mandaic
region: Southern Mesopotamia (Iraq, Khuzestan in Iran); diaspora in Australia, Sweden, US
description: Eastern Late Aramaic dialect; the liturgical and formerly vernacular language of the Mandaeans, an ancient Gnostic religious community. Classical Mandaic survives in the Ginza Rabba; Neo-Mandaic is still spoken by perhaps a few hundred as the only surviving non-Christian, non-Jewish Aramaic vernacular. Written in the distinctive Mandaic alphabet.

name: Hatran Aramaic
description: Middle Aramaic dialect of the city of Hatra and the kingdom of Arba (modern Erbil). Attested in some 500 inscriptions, mostly votive, dating from c. 100 BCE to the Sasanian destruction of Hatra in 240 CE.

name: Nabataean Aramaic
description: Middle Aramaic dialect of the Nabataean kingdom, attested in inscriptions across the Hejaz, southern Levant, and Sinai. The Nabataean script (a cursive form of Aramaic) is the direct ancestor of the Arabic script. The Nabataeans are widely thought to have been ethnically Arab and to have spoken an early form of Arabic alongside written Aramaic.

name: Palmyrene Aramaic
description: Middle Aramaic dialect of the Syrian caravan city of Palmyra, attested in several thousand inscriptions in a distinctive Palmyrene script, including bilingual Greek-Palmyrene texts.

name: Proto-Old South Arabian (Proto-Sayhadic)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Old South Arabian (Sayhadic) languages of pre-Islamic Yemen, written in the Ancient South Arabian (musnad) script. Distinct from the Modern South Arabian languages, a separate Semitic branch despite the parallel name. Position within Semitic disputed: traditionally Western/Southern, more recently sometimes Central.

name: Sabaean (Sabaic)
region: Saba (kingdom centered on Mārib, southwestern Arabian Peninsula)
description: Most extensively attested Old South Arabian language, the language of the Sabaean kingdom (capital Mārib, biblical Sheba) and later of the Himyarites who unified southern Arabia (c. 110 BCE–525 CE). Attested in thousands of inscriptions in the musnad script down to the early Islamic conquest.

name: Minaean (Madhābic)
region: Minaean kingdom (al-Jawf, northern Yemen) and caravan colonies up to Dedan (NW Arabia) and Egypt
description: Old South Arabian language of the Minaean kingdom, a major incense-trade polity. Minaean inscriptions are also found in trading colonies far to the north (Dedan/al-'Ula, Egypt, Delos).

name: Qatabanian
description: Old South Arabian language of the Qataban kingdom, a major incense-trade polity centered on Tamna'.

name: Hadramautic
description: Old South Arabian language of the Hadramaut kingdom, centered on Shabwa. Linguistically the most distinctive of the four major OSA languages.

name: Himyaritic
description: Poorly attested Late Sayhadic-period language; the spoken Himyaritic vernacular may have been distinct from the Sabaic literary/inscriptional language used by the Himyarite kings. A small corpus of post-Sabaic inscriptions and references in early Islamic-era sources suggest Himyaritic continued in spoken use into the early Islamic period.

name: Proto-Modern South Arabian
region: Southern Arabian Peninsula (Yemen, Oman) and Socotra
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Modern South Arabian (MSA) languages — Mehri, Soqotri, Shehri (Jibbali), Harsusi, Bathari, Hobyot. Despite the name, these are NOT descended from Old South Arabian; they form a separate Semitic branch, traditionally grouped with Ethio-Semitic as 'South Semitic' (a grouping disputed in some recent classifications).

name: Mehri (Mahri)
region: Eastern Yemen (Mahra), western Oman (Dhofar), southern Saudi Arabia
description: Largest Modern South Arabian language by speakers (~120,000). Highly conservative within Semitic; preserves the original three sibilants and many archaic morphological features. Unwritten in traditional use; recent ad-hoc Arabic-script orthographies.

name: Soqotri
description: Modern South Arabian language spoken on the isolated island of Socotra; phonologically and lexically the most divergent MSA language due to long isolation.

name: Shehri (Jibbali)
description: Modern South Arabian language of the Jibbali people of the Dhofar highlands.

name: Harsusi
description: Modern South Arabian language closely related to Mehri; spoken by the Harasis tribe in the central Omani desert. Severely endangered (perhaps 1,000–2,000 speakers).

name: Bathari
description: Severely endangered Modern South Arabian language; perhaps fewer than 100 speakers.

name: Hobyot (Hobi)
description: Modern South Arabian language transitional between Mehri and Shehri; severely endangered.

name: Proto-Ethio-Semitic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Ethio-Semitic languages, the result of a migration of South Semitic speakers from southern Arabia into the Horn of Africa (traditionally dated c. 1000 BCE, increasingly questioned). Splits into North Ethio-Semitic (Ge'ez, Tigre, Tigrinya) and South Ethio-Semitic (Amharic, Argobba, Harari, Gurage, Gafat).

name: Tigre (Tigrayit)
description: North Ethio-Semitic language; sister of Tigrinya and Ge'ez. Spoken by the Tigre, Beni-Amer, and Habab peoples; most speakers are Muslim. Limited literary tradition.

name: Argobba
description: South Ethio-Semitic language closely related to Amharic; spoken by the Muslim Argobba people. Severely endangered with most speakers shifting to Amharic or Afar.

name: Harari (Adare)
description: South Ethio-Semitic language of the historic walled city of Harar, a major center of Islamic learning in the Horn of Africa. Historically written in Arabic script; now also Ge'ez script and Latin.

name: Gurage languages
description: South Ethio-Semitic dialect cluster, including Sebat Bet (Chaha, Inor, etc.), Soddo, Mesqan, and others. Internal diversity is great enough that 'Gurage' is sometimes treated as several languages rather than one.

name: Gafat
description: Extinct South Ethio-Semitic language; last documented in mid-20th century when only a handful of elderly speakers remained.

name: Zay (Zway)
description: South Ethio-Semitic language closely related to Silt'e and Harari, spoken by the small Christian Zay community on the islands of Lake Zway.

name: Proto-Cushitic
region: Northeast Africa (probably Ethiopian highlands and Red Sea coast)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Cushitic branch of Afroasiatic, divided into North Cushitic (Beja), Central Cushitic (Agaw), Eastern Cushitic, and South Cushitic. The internal unity of Cushitic is generally accepted, though the placement of Beja (sometimes a separate branch) and South Cushitic (sometimes argued to be East Cushitic) is debated.

name: Proto-North Cushitic
region: Red Sea coastal Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea
description: Reconstructed ancestor of North Cushitic, comprising Beja alone. Some scholars treat Beja as a separate primary branch of Cushitic or even of Afroasiatic; included here as North Cushitic per the majority view.

name: Beja (Bedawi / Bidhaawyeet)
region: Eastern Sudan, southeastern Egypt, northern Eritrea
description: Only North Cushitic language; spoken by the Beja peoples (Bishari, Hadendoa, Ababda, Amarar, Bani Amer). Has a strong oral poetic tradition; Latin-based orthography developed in the 1980s.

name: Proto-Agaw (Proto-Central Cushitic)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Agaw (Central Cushitic) languages, the indigenous Cushitic languages of the northern Ethiopian highlands largely displaced by the spread of Ge'ez and its descendants. Major Agaw substrate in Ethio-Semitic.

name: Bilen (Blin)
description: Northernmost surviving Agaw language; spoken by the Bilen people. Ge'ez and Latin scripts used.

name: Awngi (Awi)
description: Southern Agaw language; the most vigorous of the surviving Agaw languages.

name: Kemant (Qimant)
description: Northern Agaw language; spoken by the Kemant people, traditionally adherents of a syncretic religion (sometimes called Kemantney) blending Cushitic, Ethiopian Jewish, and Christian elements. Severely endangered.

name: Kayla (Qwara)
description: Extinct or nearly extinct Northern Agaw language traditionally associated with the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jewish) community.

name: Proto-East Cushitic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of East Cushitic, the largest and most internally diverse Cushitic sub-branch. Subdivided into Highland East Cushitic (Sidamic), Lowland East Cushitic (Saho-Afar, Omo-Tana including Somali, and Oromoid), and sometimes Dullay (Tsamai, Gawwada).

name: Afar (Qafar af)
description: Lowland East Cushitic language closely related to Saho. Official language of the Afar Region of Ethiopia; widely spoken in Djibouti. Written in Latin (Qafar Feera) since 1976; previously in Ge'ez script.

name: Saho
region: Southern Eritrea and adjacent northern Ethiopia
description: Lowland East Cushitic language; closely related to Afar (the two are sometimes treated as a single Afar-Saho language). Saho speakers are predominantly Muslim and largely pastoralist.

name: Rendille
description: Lowland East Cushitic (Omo-Tana) language closely related to Somali; spoken by the camel-pastoralist Rendille people.

name: Boni (Aweer)
region: Coastal Lamu region, Kenya, and adjacent Somalia
description: Lowland East Cushitic (Omo-Tana) language of the Aweer hunter-gatherer community.

name: Dhaasanac (Daasanach)
description: Omo-Tana East Cushitic language of the Dhaasanac people of the Lake Turkana region.

name: Arbore (Hor)
description: Omo-Tana East Cushitic language closely related to Dhaasanac.

name: Elmolo
description: Omo-Tana East Cushitic language of the Elmolo fishing community; effectively extinct as a first language, with the Elmolo having shifted to Samburu (Nilotic). Some revitalization efforts underway.

name: Proto-Highland East Cushitic (Sidamic)
region: Sidama and adjacent zones, southern Ethiopia
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Highland East Cushitic / Sidamic sub-branch: Sidamo, Hadiyya, Kambaata, Burji, Alaba, K'abeena, Gedeo (Derasa).

name: Sidamo (Sidaama)
description: Largest Highland East Cushitic language; official working language of the Sidama Region. Written in Latin script.

name: Hadiyya
description: Highland East Cushitic language; written in Latin script.

name: Kambaata (Kambaatissata)
description: Highland East Cushitic language; closely related to Hadiyya and Alaba.

name: Burji
region: Burji Special Woreda, southern Ethiopia; northern Kenya
description: Southernmost Highland East Cushitic language; geographically isolated from other HEC languages by Omotic and Lowland East Cushitic languages.

name: Alaba (Alaaba)
description: Highland East Cushitic language closely related to Kambaata; sometimes treated as a dialect of Kambaata.

name: Gedeo (Derasa)
description: Highland East Cushitic language; speakers practice the Songo religion alongside Ethiopian Orthodoxy and Protestantism. Famous for traditional intensive agroforestry coffee-cultivation.

name: Proto-Oromoid
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Oromo and Konso-Gidole; sometimes grouped with Omo-Tana into a 'Macro-Oromoid' or with Yaaku into a more inclusive subgroup.

name: Konso (Xonsoo)
description: Oromoid East Cushitic language of the Konso people, known for terraced highland agriculture and walled villages (UNESCO World Heritage).

name: Proto-South Cushitic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of South Cushitic, the southernmost Cushitic outlier in eastern Africa. Includes Iraqw, Gorowa, Alagwa, Burunge, and the extinct Aasáx and Kw'adza. Some scholars argue South Cushitic is in fact a subgroup of East Cushitic rather than an independent branch.

name: Iraqw
region: Mbulu and Karatu districts, Arusha Region, Tanzania
description: Largest South Cushitic language; the Iraqw people are agriculturalists of the Tanzanian Rift Valley. Distinctive among Cushitic for having lost most laryngeal phonemes.

name: Gorowa
description: South Cushitic language closely related to Iraqw; sometimes treated as a dialect of Iraqw.

name: Alagwa
description: South Cushitic language closely related to Iraqw.

name: Burunge
description: South Cushitic language; endangered with most speakers shifting to Swahili.

name: Dahalo
region: Lower Tana River area, coastal Kenya
description: South Cushitic language remarkable for retaining click consonants (dental, alveolar, lateral), interpreted as a substrate from a pre-Cushitic Khoisan-related population once present in East Africa. Severely endangered with fewer than 400 speakers.

name: Proto-Omotic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Omotic languages. Its position within Afroasiatic is disputed: most Africanists (Bender, Hayward) accept it as the most divergent AA branch; others (Theil) argue it is not Afroasiatic at all. Internal subdivisions: North Omotic (Ometo, Gimira, Yem, Kafa-Gonga, Dizoid) and South Omotic (Aroid).

name: Proto-North Omotic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of North Omotic, comprising Ometo (Wolaytta, Gamo, Gofa, Dawro, Basketo, Male, etc.), Gimira (Bench, Sheko), Yem, Kafa-Gonga (Kafa, Shekkacho, Anfillo, Boro), and Dizoid (Dizi, Sheko, Nayi).

name: Wolaytta (Wolaitta)
description: Largest Omotic language; the Wolaitta kingdom was a major polity of southern Ethiopia conquered by Menelik II in 1894. Written in Latin script. Mutually intelligible to varying degrees with several other Ometo varieties (Gamo, Gofa, Dawro).

name: Gamo
description: Ometo Omotic language closely related to Wolaytta; sometimes treated as a Wolaytta dialect, sometimes as a separate language. The Gamo highlands are famous for traditional democratic council-based governance.

name: Gofa
description: Ometo Omotic language closely related to Wolaytta and Gamo.

name: Dawro
description: Ometo Omotic language closely related to Wolaytta.

name: Kafa (Kafa-Kefa)
description: Major Kafa-Gonga (North Omotic) language. The Kingdom of Kaffa was one of the largest and longest-lasting independent African polities, surviving until 1897. Reputed origin of cultivated coffee (Coffea arabica).

name: Dizi (Dizin)
region: Bench Maji and West Omo Zones, southwestern Ethiopia
description: Dizoid North Omotic language; classification of Dizoid (Dizi, Sheko, Nayi) as North Omotic vs. a separate branch is debated.

name: Proto-South Omotic (Proto-Aroid)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the South Omotic / Aroid languages: Aari, Hamer-Banna, Karo, Dime. The unity of Aroid is secure; its inclusion within Omotic (vs. as a separate Afroasiatic branch or non-AA family) is debated alongside the broader Omotic controversy.

name: Aari (Ari)
description: Largest South Omotic language; spoken by the agriculturalist Aari people of the Bako region.

name: Hamer (Hamer-Banna)
description: South Omotic language of the Hamer agropastoralists of the Lower Omo Valley; closely related to Banna and Karo.

name: Maale (Male)
description: Ometo Omotic language transitional between the Ometo cluster and South Omotic in some respects.

name: Riffian (Tarifit)
