region: Rif mountains, northern Morocco; diaspora in Spain, Belgium, Netherlands
description: Northern Berber language of the Rif region; major Berber variety with c. 1.5 million speakers in Morocco and large European diaspora populations.

name: Shilha (Tashelhit)
region: Souss valley and Anti-Atlas, southwestern Morocco
description: Largest Berber variety; spoken by the Ishelhin (Chleuh) of southwestern Morocco. Has a substantial pre-modern literary tradition in Arabic script (Tashelhit manuscripts from at least the 16th century).

name: Shawiya (Tachawit)
description: Northern Berber language of the Chaoui people; closely related to Kabyle. The Aurès was the heartland of the 7th-century Berber resistance to the Arab conquest led by Kahina.

name: Siwi (Siwa Berber)
region: Siwa Oasis, Western Desert of Egypt
description: Easternmost surviving Berber language; an isolate within Berber spoken in the oasis of Siwa, surrounded by Arabic-speaking populations. Substantial Arabic borrowings.

name: Zenaga
description: Highly divergent and endangered Berber language of southwestern Mauritania; the southernmost Berber variety. Once widespread before being largely displaced by Hassaniya Arabic from the 17th century onward; now perhaps 200 speakers.

name: Ghadamès (Ghadamsi)
description: Northern Berber language of the Ghadamès oasis. Phonologically conservative and lexically distinctive due to long isolation.

name: Nafusi
description: Northern Berber language closely related to Zuwara; the Nafusa region is historically associated with Ibadi Islam.

name: Guanche
description: Extinct Berber language(s) of the indigenous Guanche of the Canary Islands, attested in inscriptions in a script related to Tifinagh and in a limited vocabulary recorded by Spanish colonizers. Speakers were largely killed or assimilated during the Castilian conquest of the Canaries (1402–1496).

name: Numidian (Libyco-Berber)
description: Ancestral Berber language(s) of the Numidian kingdoms (Massyli, Masaesyli, including the kingdoms of Massinissa and Jugurtha). Attested in Libyco-Berber inscriptions in a script that is the ancestor of Tifinagh.

name: Tifinagh script (Old Libyco-Berber)
description: Note: Tifinagh is properly a script rather than a language. Included here as the writing-system continuum from ancient Libyco-Berber inscriptions through to modern Neo-Tifinagh, adopted as the official Berber script in Morocco (2003). Preserved most continuously by Tuareg communities while most Berber speech communities shifted to Arabic script.

name: Proto-Chadic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Chadic branch, the largest Afroasiatic branch by number of languages (~150–200). Subdivided into West Chadic (Hausa and many others), Biu-Mandara/Central Chadic, East Chadic, and Masa.

name: Bole
region: Yobe and Gombe States, northeastern Nigeria
description: West Chadic language closely related to Hausa; historically associated with the Bornu-allied Bole-Tangale states.

name: Ngas (Angas)
description: West Chadic language; Angas is the older English name.

name: Mwaghavul (Sura)
description: West Chadic language closely related to Ngas.

name: Kotoko languages
description: Central Chadic (Biu-Mandara) dialect cluster of the Kotoko city-states region; long-standing contact with Kanuri and Chadic Arabic.

name: Kanakuru (Dera)
description: West Chadic language famous in phonological theory for its complex tonal system.

name: Musgu (Mulwi)
region: Far North Cameroon and southwestern Chad
description: Central Chadic language of the Musgu people.

name: Mubi
description: East Chadic language of the Mubi people.

name: Masa (Masana)
description: Type language of the Masa branch of Chadic (sometimes grouped with Central Chadic).

name: Proto-Atayalic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Atayalic branch of Austronesian, comprising Atayal and Seediq. One of ~9–10 primary branches of Austronesian recognized by Blust; all but Malayo-Polynesian are confined to Taiwan, making the family's primary diversification a Taiwan-internal phenomenon.

name: Atayal (Tayal)
region: Northern Taiwanese mountains (Hsinchu, Miaoli, Taichung, Nantou, Yilan, Hualien)
description: Largest Atayalic language; second-largest Formosan-language community. Speakers traditionally practiced facial tattooing as a rite of passage. Highly dialectally diverse: Squliq is the literary basis.

name: Seediq (Truku)
description: Atayalic language; Truku (Taroko) was formerly classified as a Seediq dialect but recognized as a separate ethnic group by Taiwan in 2004. Subject of the 1930 Wushe Incident (Seediq Bale).

name: Proto-Rukai
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Rukai branch, a primary Austronesian branch consisting of Rukai alone. Notable for being one of two Formosan branches (alongside Tsouic) lacking the otherwise pan-AN Philippine-type voice/focus system.

name: Rukai
region: Pingtung and Taitung counties, southern Taiwan
description: Sole surviving Rukai language; multiple dialects (Tanan, Budai, Labuan, Maga, Tona, Mantauran) with significant internal variation. Mantauran Rukai is the most divergent.

name: Proto-Tsouic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tsouic branch, comprising Tsou, Kanakanavu, and Saaroa. Treated by Blust as a single primary branch; recent work (Ross, Chang) increasingly treats Tsou and the Southern Tsouic languages (Kanakanavu, Saaroa) as separate primary branches, making 'Tsouic' paraphyletic.

name: Tsou (Cou)
region: Chiayi County and Nantou County, Taiwan (around Yushan/Mt. Jade)
description: Northern Tsouic language. Like Rukai, lacks the Philippine-type voice system that characterizes most Austronesian languages, a feature of major typological importance for reconstructing Proto-Austronesian.

name: Kanakanavu
description: Southern Tsouic language; severely endangered with fewer than 10 fluent speakers.

name: Saaroa (Hla'alua)
description: Southern Tsouic language; severely endangered.

name: Proto-East Formosan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the East Formosan branch (Amis, Siraya, Kavalan, Basay-Trobiawan). Validity as a single clade is debated; Blust treats it as a primary AN branch.

name: Amis (Pangcah)
description: Largest Formosan language by speakers (~190,000 ethnic Amis, perhaps half retaining the language). Multiple dialects (Northern, Central, Southern, Sakizaya — Sakizaya recognized as a separate ethnic group in 2007).

name: Kavalan
description: Lowland Formosan language; the Kavalan were displaced from the Yilan plain by Han Chinese settlement in the 19th century and resettled in Hualien. Severely endangered.

name: Siraya
description: Plains Formosan language of the Siraya people; extensively documented by 17th-century Dutch colonial missionaries, including a Gospel of Matthew translation (1661). The Sinckan Manuscripts (land deeds in Sirayan script) continued in Siraya through the 19th century. Effectively extinct from c. 1900; revitalization underway since the 1990s.

name: Proto-Northwest Formosan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Northwest Formosan branch (Saisiyat, Pazeh-Kulon, Thao in some classifications). Status as a single clade is debated.

name: Saisiyat
description: Northwest Formosan language. The Saisiyat are famous for the biennial Pas-ta'ai ritual commemorating the legendary 'short black people' (Ta'ai).

name: Pazeh (Pazih)
description: Plains Formosan language; last fluent speaker Pan Jin-yu died in 2010. Some revitalization efforts in the Pazeh community.

name: Thao
region: Sun Moon Lake region, Nantou County, Taiwan
description: Highly endangered Formosan language; perhaps a dozen fluent speakers. Branch affiliation disputed; some classifications place Thao with Northwest Formosan, others as its own branch.

name: Proto-Western Plains (Proto-Babuza-Taokas)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Western Plains Formosan branch (Babuza, Taokas, Papora, Hoanya). All Western Plains languages are extinct, most from before c. 1900.

name: Babuza
region: Changhua and Yunlin coastal plain, western Taiwan
description: Extinct Western Plains Formosan language; documented in 19th-century Dutch and Spanish missionary materials and later Japanese fieldwork.

name: Taokas
region: Hsinchu and Miaoli coastal plain, Taiwan
description: Extinct Western Plains Formosan language.

name: Proto-Bunun
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Bunun branch, a primary Austronesian branch consisting of Bunun alone.

name: Bunun
region: Central mountain ranges of Taiwan (Nantou, Hualien, Taitung, Kaohsiung)
description: Sole Bunun language; five recognized dialects (Takbanuaz, Takivatan, Takibakha, Takituduh, Isbukun). Famous for the Pasibutbut, a polyphonic ritual chant of unusual structural complexity.

name: Proto-Paiwanic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Paiwan alone; primary AN branch in Blust's classification.

name: Paiwan
description: Third-largest Formosan language by speakers. Distinctive class system in nominal morphology; speakers historically organized into stratified society with hereditary chiefs.

name: Proto-Puyuma
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Puyuma; in Ross's classification, Puyuma is one of the most divergent Austronesian languages and one of the keys to PAn reconstruction.

name: Puyuma (Pinuyumayan)
description: Formosan language closely studied for its conservative voice system. The Nanwang dialect retains many features posited for Proto-Austronesian.

name: Proto-Central-Eastern Malayo-Polynesian
description: Reconstructed intermediate ancestor in Blust's classification of Austronesian. Comprises Central MP (Lesser Sundas, Maluku) and Eastern MP. The Western/CEMP split has been challenged in recent work (e.g., Donohue–Grimes), but remains the standard framework.

name: Proto-Central Malayo-Polynesian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Central Malayo-Polynesian languages of the Lesser Sundas (Timor, Flores, Sumba, Sumbawa east of the Bima isogloss) and southern Maluku (Aru, Kei, Tanimbar). Unity of Central MP is debated; some treat it as a geographic grouping rather than a clade.

name: Proto-Eastern Malayo-Polynesian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Eastern MP, splitting into South Halmahera-West New Guinea (SHWNG) and Oceanic.

name: Proto-South Halmahera-West New Guinea
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the South Halmahera-West New Guinea languages, Eastern MP languages spoken outside Oceania. Closest extant non-Oceanic relatives of the Oceanic family.

name: Proto-Philippine
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Philippine languages. The 'Philippine subgroup' hypothesis (Blust) treats them as a clade; Ross and Reid argue they do not, treating 'Philippine' as a geographic linkage of primary Malayo-Polynesian subgroups. Includes Northern (Ilocano, Pangasinan), Central (Tagalog, Bikol, Visayan), and Southern Philippine.

name: Bikol (Central Bikol)
description: Central Philippine language; major lingua franca of the Bicol Region. Subject of Spanish colonial-era documentation and a substantial pre-modern literary tradition.

name: Hiligaynon (Ilonggo)
description: Western Visayan language; one of the major Philippine languages by speakers (~9 million). Capital city Iloilo.

name: Waray (Waray-Waray, Samar-Leyte)
description: Eastern Visayan language; major Philippine language with ~3.5 million speakers.

name: Kapampangan (Pampangan)
region: Pampanga and surrounding Central Luzon, Philippines
description: Central Luzon language; speakers historically formed the elite of the Spanish colonial military in the Philippines.

name: Pangasinan
description: Northern Philippine language closely related to Ilocano. The pre-colonial Pangasinan polity was a significant Luzon kingdom.

name: Tausug (Sūg)
description: Central Philippine language closely related to Visayan; the language of the Sultanate of Sulu (c. 1457–1915). Written historically in the Jawi (Arabic-script) Tausug orthography.

name: Maranao
region: Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte, Mindanao, Philippines
description: Danao subgroup (Southern Mindanao) Philippine language; written in Latin and historically in the Kirim (Arabic-script) orthography. The Maranao are predominantly Muslim and were never fully subjugated by Spain.

name: Maguindanao
description: Danao subgroup Philippine language; the language of the Sultanate of Maguindanao (c. 1500–1899).

name: Yakan
region: Basilan and surrounding Sulu Archipelago, Philippines
description: Sama-Bajaw Philippine language; Yakan is sometimes treated separately from Sama-Bajaw proper.

name: Ibanag
description: Northern Philippine (Northern Cordilleran) language; major language of the Cagayan Valley.

name: Proto-Greater Barito
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Greater Barito subgroup: Sama-Bajaw (debated), East Barito (Maanyan, etc. — closest mainland relatives of Malagasy), and West Barito (Ngaju Dayak). Speakers of an East Barito variety close to Maanyan are the ancestors of the Malagasy, having migrated to Madagascar from southern Borneo c. 500–1000 CE.

name: Maanyan
description: East Barito language; widely regarded as the closest mainland relative of Malagasy, supporting the southern Borneo origin of the Malagasy.

name: Ngaju (Ngaju Dayak)
description: Major West Barito language; one of the largest Dayak languages by speakers.

name: Proto-Western Oceanic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Western Oceanic subgroup (North New Guinea, Papuan Tip, Meso-Melanesian linkages). Validity as a clade vs. a linkage is debated.

name: Proto-Admiralty
region: Admiralty Islands (Manus Province, Papua New Guinea)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Admiralty subgroup, one of the most divergent Oceanic groups.

name: Proto-Central-Eastern Oceanic
region: Solomon Islands east through Remote Oceania
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Central-Eastern Oceanic, encompassing Southeast Solomonic, Northern and Central Vanuatu, Southern Vanuatu, New Caledonian, Micronesian, and Central Pacific (Fijian-Polynesian).

name: Proto-Southeast Solomonic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Southeast Solomonic languages: Guadalcanal-Nggela, Malaita-Makira, and others.

name: Proto-Central Pacific
region: Fiji and adjacent areas (Lapita cultural complex)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Central Pacific subgroup, splitting into West Fijian-Rotuman and East Fijian-Polynesian. The Lapita pottery culture (c. 1500–500 BCE) is generally associated with the Proto-Central Pacific speech community.

name: Rotuman
description: Central Pacific language closely related to but distinct from Fijian; spoken on the isolated island of Rotuma, politically part of Fiji but culturally distinct. Famous for its system of 'incomplete phase' vs. 'complete phase' word forms produced by metathesis/vowel-loss.

name: Proto-Micronesian (Nuclear Micronesian)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Nuclear Micronesian languages. Does NOT include Chamorro or Palauan, which are independent Malayo-Polynesian primary branches that reached Micronesia from the west; Nuclear Micronesian languages reached Micronesia from the southeast (Vanuatu/Solomons area) much later.

name: Marshallese (Kajin M̧ajeļ)
region: Marshall Islands; diaspora in Hawaii, Arkansas, Oklahoma
description: Eastern Micronesian language; official language of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Two dialects (Rālik, Ratak) corresponding to the two atoll chains.

name: Gilbertese (Kiribati / Taetae ni Kiribati)
region: Kiribati, Nauru (as second language), Fiji (Rabi I.), Solomon Is.
description: Official language of Kiribati; the most widely spoken Micronesian language. The country name 'Kiribati' is the Gilbertese pronunciation of 'Gilberts'.

name: Pohnpeian (Mahsen en Pohnpei)
description: Chuukic-Pohnpeic language; official language of Pohnpei state. Distinctive honorific register (meing) used in formal speech.

name: Chuukese (Trukese / Fóósun Chuuk)
description: Largest Chuukic-Pohnpeic language by speakers. Part of a dialect continuum that includes Mortlockese, Pulapese, and several other Chuukic varieties.

name: Kosraean (Kosrae)
description: Distinctive Micronesian language; most divergent of the Nuclear Micronesian languages, sometimes treated as a primary branch.

name: Nauruan (Dorerin Naoero)
description: Sole indigenous language of Nauru; official language alongside English. Position within Micronesian disputed: sometimes treated as a primary Micronesian branch, sometimes grouped with Marshallese.

name: Yapese (Thin nu Wa'ab)
description: Oceanic language whose precise subgrouping is unresolved — not a Nuclear Micronesian language. Yap's stone-money system and pre-colonial empire over surrounding Caroline atolls (the Yap Empire) are distinctive cultural features.

name: Palauan (a tekoi er a Belau)
description: Primary Malayo-Polynesian language, NOT Micronesian; reached Palau directly from western Indonesia or the Philippines. Often grouped with Chamorro as 'Western Malayo-Polynesian outliers' though this grouping is not strongly supported. Official language of Palau alongside English.

name: Proto-Polynesian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Polynesian languages, descended from a Central Pacific (Fijian-Polynesian) ancestor near western Polynesia. Splits into Tongic (Tongan, Niuean) and Nuclear Polynesian. The Polynesian Triangle (Aotearoa–Rapa Nui–Hawai'i) was colonized from this homeland in migrations from c. 1000 BCE through c. 1300 CE.

name: Proto-Tongic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tongic branch of Polynesian, comprising Tongan and Niuean. Tongic preserves Proto-Polynesian *h, lost in Nuclear Polynesian, and a number of other conservative features.

name: Niuean (ko e vagahau Niue)
region: Niue; large diaspora in New Zealand
description: Tongic Polynesian language; co-official language of Niue. Two main dialects (Motu, Tafiti).

name: Proto-Nuclear Polynesian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Nuclear Polynesian languages (i.e., all Polynesian languages except Tongan and Niuean). Splits into Samoic-Outlier and Eastern Polynesian.

name: Proto-Samoic-Outlier
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Samoic-Outlier subgroup: Samoan, Tokelauan, Tuvaluan, Wallisian, Futunan, and the Polynesian Outlier languages — Polynesian enclaves in Melanesia and Micronesia (Tikopia, Anuta, Rennell-Bellona, Nukuoro, etc.) thought to result from back-migrations from western Polynesia. Validity as a single clade is debated.

name: Tokelauan (Gagana Tokelau)
region: Tokelau; large diaspora in New Zealand
description: Samoic Polynesian language; mutually intelligible to a significant degree with Tuvaluan and Samoan.

name: Tuvaluan (Te 'gana Tūvalu)
description: Samoic Polynesian language; co-official language of Tuvalu. Two main dialect groups: Northern (Nanumea, Niutao, Nanumaga) and Southern (Vaitupu, Nukufetau, Funafuti, Nukulaelae). Closely related to Tokelauan.

name: Wallisian (East Uvean / Faka'uvea)
description: Samoic Polynesian language closely related to Tongan and Samoan. Co-official language of Wallis and Futuna alongside French.

name: Futunan (East Futunan / Fakafutuna)
region: Futuna and Alofi, Wallis and Futuna (France)
description: Samoic Polynesian language; closely related to but distinct from Wallisian.

name: Tikopia
region: Tikopia Island, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
description: Polynesian Outlier language of the Tikopia, a Polynesian-speaking community in Melanesia. Subject of Raymond Firth's classic ethnography 'We, the Tikopia' (1936).

name: Rennellese (Mu Gangoa)
region: Rennell and Bellona Islands, Solomon Islands
description: Polynesian Outlier language of Rennell and Bellona islands; documented in detail by Samuel Elbert.

name: Proto-Eastern Polynesian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Eastern Polynesian languages, encompassing the languages of all the islands in the eastern Polynesian Triangle (Society, Cook, Tuamotu, Marquesas, Hawai'i, Aotearoa, Rapa Nui). Splits into Rapa Nui (most divergent), Tahitic, and Marquesic.

name: Proto-Tahitic (Central Eastern)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tahitic subgroup of Eastern Polynesian: Tahitian, Cook Islands Māori (Rarotongan), New Zealand Māori, Tuamotuan, and others.

name: Proto-Marquesic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Marquesic subgroup: Marquesan, Hawaiian, Mangarevan.

name: Marquesan (ʻEo Enana / ʻEo Enata)
description: Marquesic Polynesian language; the Marquesas Islands are thought to have been a major dispersal point for the colonization of Hawai'i and Easter Island. Two dialects (North Marquesan, South Marquesan).

name: Mangarevan (Mangareva)
description: Marquesic Polynesian language; speakers were the launching population for the colonization of Henderson, Pitcairn, and possibly other isolated southeastern Polynesian islands.

name: Cook Islands Māori (Rarotongan)
description: Tahitic Polynesian language; co-official language of the Cook Islands alongside English. Closely related to New Zealand Māori (the Māori traditionally trace their migration to Aotearoa from Rarotonga and other Cook/Society Islands departure points).

name: Tuamotuan (Reo Pa'umotu)
description: Tahitic Polynesian language; the Pa'umotu people inhabit the largest archipelago of low-lying atolls in the world. Heavily influenced by Tahitian.

name: Tolai (Kuanua / Tinata Tuna)
region: Gazelle Peninsula, East New Britain, Papua New Guinea
description: Meso-Melanesian Oceanic language; the most widely spoken indigenous language of East New Britain. Loanwords from Tolai entered Tok Pisin during the German colonial period.

name: Motu (Pure Motu / True Motu)
region: Central Province, Papua New Guinea (around Port Moresby)
description: Papuan Tip Oceanic language. The basis for Hiri Motu (Police Motu), a pidginized variety formerly a colonial-era trade lingua franca and a co-official language of Papua New Guinea.

name: Nakanai (Lakalai)
region: Northern coast of West New Britain, Papua New Guinea
description: Meso-Melanesian Oceanic language.

name: Mussau (Mussau-Emira)
region: Mussau and Emira islands (St. Matthias group), New Ireland Province, PNG
description: Admiralties Oceanic language; documented extensively by Malcolm Ross and others.

name: Tetum (Tetun)
description: Central Malayo-Polynesian language; co-official language of Timor-Leste alongside Portuguese. Two main varieties: Tetun-Terik (vernacular, conservative) and Tetun-Dili / Tetun Prasa (creolized urban lingua franca with heavy Portuguese influence), the latter being the basis of the official standard.

name: Proto-Oghur (Proto-Bulgar)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Oghur (Bulgaric, Lir-Turkic) branch of Turkic, marked by *r/*l where Common Turkic shows *z/*ş in cognates. The first Turkic branch to split off from Proto-Turkic. Historically the language of the Onogur, Sabir, Khazar, and Volga Bulgar peoples; only Chuvash survives.

name: Proto-Common Turkic (Proto-Shaz-Turkic)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of all Turkic languages except the Oghur (Bulgaric) branch. Splits into the major modern branches: Karluk, Kipchak, Oghuz, Siberian (paraphyletic), Arghu (Khalaj), and various extinct intermediate stages including Old Turkic, Old Uyghur, and Karakhanid.

name: Volga Bolgar (Volga Bulgar)
region: Middle Volga (Tatarstan, Chuvashia, Bashkortostan, Mari El)
description: Extinct Oghur Turkic language of the Volga Bulgar state (c. 660s–1240s CE) and its post-Mongol successors, attested in funerary inscriptions in Arabic script (13th–14th c.). Sister of Chuvash within Oghur. The Islamic Volga Bulgars are partial ancestors of the modern Volga Tatars and Chuvash, though the Tatars later shifted to a Kipchak language.

name: Khazar
region: Khazar Khaganate (North Caucasus, Pontic-Caspian steppe, lower Volga)
description: Probably extinct Turkic language of the Khazar Khaganate (c. 650–969 CE), whose ruling elite famously converted to Judaism around 800 CE. Affiliation debated due to scarce evidence; the majority view (Golden, Pritsak) places Khazar in Oghur Turkic, but some argue for Common Turkic or a non-Turkic substrate. Attested only in fragments and names.

name: Proto-Karluk
region: Inner Asia (Karluk Yabghu state, Karakhanid Khaganate)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Karluk (Chagatai, Southeastern) branch of Turkic. The Karakhanid Khaganate (840–1212 CE) was the first major Turkic Muslim state and produced the earliest Islamic Turkic literature (al-Kashgari's Dīwān, 1077; Yusuf Khass Hajib's Kutadgu Bilig, 1069). Modern descendants: Uyghur, Uzbek, Aini, and partially Salar.

name: Karakhanid (Khaqani Turkic)
region: Karakhanid Khaganate (Transoxiana, Tarim Basin, eastern Turkestan)
description: Karluk Turkic literary language of the Karakhanid state, written in Arabic script. Key works include Mahmud al-Kashgari's Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk (1072–1077, a comparative Turkic dictionary and one of the most important sources for early Turkic linguistics) and the Kutadgu Bilig of Yusuf Khass Hajib (1069/1070).

name: Old Uyghur
description: Literary and religious language of the Uyghur kingdoms in the Tarim Basin after the Uyghur Khaganate's collapse in 840 CE. Attested in Buddhist, Manichaean, and Christian texts in the Sogdian-derived Old Uyghur script. NOT the direct ancestor of modern Uyghur (a Karluk language); the shared ethnonym was revived for political reasons in 1921.

name: Chagatai (Türki)
region: Central Asia (Chagatai Khanate territories and successors)
description: Karluk Turkic literary language used across Central Asia from c. 14th to early 20th century, named for Chagatai Khan. Standardized in the late 15th century under the Timurid renaissance; reached its classical form in the works of Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i (1441–1501). Replaced by modern standardized Uzbek and Uyghur in the 1920s–1930s.

name: Aini (Ainu / Abdal)
description: Highly mixed Karluk Turkic language spoken by the Abdal people, a marginalized Sufi/dervish community in southern Xinjiang. Lexicon is largely Persian; grammar and core vocabulary are Karluk Turkic close to Uyghur. Not to be confused with the unrelated Ainu language of Hokkaido.

name: Salar
region: Xunhua Salar Autonomous County (Qinghai) and adjacent Gansu, China
description: Turkic language traditionally classified as Oghuz but with substantial Karluk and Tibeto-Mongolic influence; the Salars trace their origin to a 14th-century migration from Samarkand to the Tibetan plateau. Speakers are predominantly Muslim. Documented in detail by Erika Kasai and others.

name: Proto-Kipchak
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kipchak (Northwestern) branch of Turkic. Splits into Kipchak-Bulgar (Volga-Ural), Kipchak-Cuman (Caucasian and Black Sea), and Kipchak-Nogai (Aralo-Caspian and Kyrgyz-Kipchak). Speakers historically organized as the Kipchak/Cuman confederacy (11th–13th c.) across the western steppe.

name: Cuman (Kipchak / Polovtsian)
region: Pontic-Caspian steppe; Hungary; medieval Egypt (Mamluk court)
description: Medieval Kipchak Turkic language of the Cuman-Kipchak confederacy. Best documented in the Codex Cumanicus (c. 1294–1303, Crimea), a Latin-script trilingual phrasebook for Italian merchants and Franciscan missionaries. Cuman speakers settled in Hungary and the Balkans after the Mongol invasions; Cuman survived in Hungary into the 18th century.

name: Proto-Kipchak-Bulgar (Volga-Ural Kipchak)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Volga-Ural Kipchak sub-branch: Tatar (Volga, Siberian Tatar varieties) and Bashkir. The label 'Bulgar' is a historical reference to the Volga Bulgar polity in whose former territory these Kipchak languages developed after the Mongol period; the speakers' linguistic ancestors were Kipchak rather than Oghur Bulgar.

name: Proto-Kipchak-Cuman (Ponto-Caspian Kipchak)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Cuman/Polovtsian sub-branch of Kipchak: Crimean Tatar (excluding the Oghuz-influenced southern coastal varieties), Karachay-Balkar, Kumyk, Karaim, and Krymchak.

name: Proto-Kipchak-Nogai (Aralo-Caspian Kipchak)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Aralo-Caspian Kipchak sub-branch: Kazakh, Karakalpak, Nogai, and (more controversially) Kyrgyz, which is sometimes classified instead as Kyrgyz-Kipchak (a separate subgroup) or as transitional with Siberian Turkic.

name: Crimean Tatar (Qırımtatar tili)
region: Crimea; diaspora in Uzbekistan, Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria, Ukraine
description: Kipchak Cuman Turkic language with three main dialect zones: Northern (Steppe, closest to Nogai), Central (the prestige variety, used as the basis for the standard), and Southern (Yalıboyu, heavily Oghuz-influenced through Ottoman contact). Subject to mass deportation by Stalin in 1944 (the Sürgünlik); only allowed to return to Crimea from 1989.

name: Karachay-Balkar
description: Kipchak Cuman language of the Karachay and Balkar peoples, two closely related Turkic groups in the northern Caucasus. Both were collectively deported by Stalin in 1943–1944; allowed to return in 1957.

name: Kumyk (Qumuq)
description: Kipchak Cuman Turkic language; historically a major lingua franca of the northern Caucasus alongside Azerbaijani.

name: Karaim (Karay)
description: Kipchak Cuman Turkic language of the Karaim, a small Karaite Jewish community traditionally settled by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in Trakai in the 14th century. Critically endangered with fewer than 100 speakers. Traditionally written in Hebrew characters, latterly in Latin and Cyrillic.

name: Krymchak
description: Kipchak Cuman Turkic language of the Krymchak Jews (Rabbanite Jewish community of Crimea, distinct from the Karaim). Effectively extinct following the Holocaust (most of the c. 7,000 Krymchaks were murdered by the Nazis in 1941–1942) and subsequent assimilation. Traditionally written in Hebrew script.

name: Nogai (Noğay)
region: Dagestan, Karachay-Cherkessia, Stavropol Krai (Russia); diaspora in Turkey, Romania
description: Kipchak Nogai language of the Nogai people, descendants of the Nogai Horde (c. 1390–1634, a major post-Golden Horde polity of the Pontic-Caspian steppe).

name: Karakalpak (Qaraqalpaq)
description: Kipchak Nogai language closely related to Kazakh; the official language of the Karakalpakstan autonomous republic.

name: Siberian Tatar
description: Kipchak language sometimes treated as a dialect of Volga Tatar and sometimes as a separate language; phonologically and lexically intermediate between Volga Tatar and Kazakh.

name: Proto-Oghuz
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Oghuz (Southwestern) branch of Turkic. Splits into Western Oghuz (Turkish, Azerbaijani, Gagauz), Eastern Oghuz (Turkmen, Khorasani Turkic), and Southern Oghuz (Salar). Oghuz speakers entered the Middle East in the 11th c. via the Seljuk migrations and spread across Anatolia, the Caucasus, Iran, and the Balkans.

name: Gagauz
description: Western Oghuz Turkic language of the Gagauz, a Turkic-speaking but Orthodox Christian community traditionally located on the Black Sea coast. Heavily influenced by Bulgarian, Romanian, and Russian. Official language of the Gagauzia autonomous region of Moldova alongside Romanian and Russian.

name: Balkan Gagauz Turkish
region: European Turkey, northeastern Greece, southeastern Bulgaria
description: Western Oghuz Turkic language sometimes treated as part of Gagauz, sometimes as a Turkish dialect; spoken by the Surguch, Karamanli (Anatolian Greek-script Turkish), and Gajal communities. Karamanli Turkish is historically notable for having been written in the Greek alphabet by Anatolian Orthodox Christians.

name: Khorasani Turkic
description: Eastern Oghuz Turkic language transitional between Azerbaijani and Turkmen; sometimes classified as one of them rather than a separate language.

name: Qashqai (Qashqā'ī)
description: Oghuz Turkic language of the Qashqai confederation, a traditionally nomadic confederation of southern Iran. Close to Azerbaijani.

name: Cypriot Turkish (Kıbrıs Türkçesi)
region: Northern Cyprus and Cypriot diaspora in the UK
description: Oghuz Turkic variety descended from the 16th-century Anatolian Turkish brought to Cyprus by Ottoman settlers. Distinct from but mutually intelligible with Standard Turkish; heavy Greek substrate from Cypriot Greek contact.

name: Proto-Siberian Turkic
description: Convenience parent node for the geographically Siberian Turkic varieties. Not a single clade: comprises at least Yenisei Turkic (Khakas, Shor, Chulym, Fuyu Kyrgyz), Sayan Turkic (Tuvan, Tofa), Lena Turkic (Yakut/Sakha, Dolgan), and Altai Turkic. Internal subgrouping is one of the major unresolved questions in Turkic classification.

name: Proto-Sayan Turkic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Sayan Turkic sub-branch: Tuvan, Tofa (Tofalar), and the closely related and severely endangered Tsengel Tuvan and Dukha (Tsaatan) varieties of northwestern Mongolia.

name: Tofa (Tofalar / Karagas)
region: Eastern Sayan Mountains, Irkutsk Oblast, Russia
description: Critically endangered Sayan Turkic language closely related to Tuvan; spoken by the Tofalar, a small reindeer-herding people. Perhaps fewer than 100 speakers.

name: Dukha (Tsaatan)
description: Critically endangered Sayan Turkic language closely related to Tuvan; spoken by the Tsaatan, a small reindeer-herding people in northern Mongolia.

name: Proto-Yenisei Turkic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Yenisei Turkic sub-branch: Khakas, Shor, Chulym, and Fuyu Kyrgyz (an isolated migrant variety in Heilongjiang, China).

name: Khakas
description: Yenisei Turkic language of the Khakas people. Several mutually intelligible dialect groups (Sagai, Kacha, Beltir, Koibal); standardization based on Sagai. The Yenisei Kyrgyz (the historical Kyrgyz Khaganate, distinct from the modern Kyrgyz of Kyrgyzstan) are the ancestral population.

name: Shor
description: Yenisei Turkic language closely related to Khakas; severely endangered with most speakers shifting to Russian.

name: Chulym (Chulym Tatar)
region: Chulym River basin, Tomsk Oblast, Russia
description: Critically endangered Yenisei Turkic language; fewer than 100 fluent speakers.

name: Fuyu Kyrgyz (Fu-yu Gïrgïs)
description: Critically endangered Yenisei Turkic language of an isolated community in northeastern China; descendants of Yenisei Kyrgyz deported to Manchuria by the Dzungars or Qing in the 18th century. Despite the name, NOT closely related to modern Kyrgyz (a Kipchak language); Fuyu Kyrgyz is closest to Khakas. Perhaps a dozen elderly speakers remain.

name: Proto-Lena Turkic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Lena Turkic sub-branch: Yakut (Sakha) and Dolgan. Lena Turkic is the most divergent Common Turkic subgroup, with massive Mongolic and Tungusic contact influence and unique sound changes.

name: Dolgan (Dulgan / Saxa)
description: Lena Turkic language closely related to Yakut; the Dolgan ethnogenesis (c. 17th–19th c.) involved Yakut, Evenki (Tungusic), Russian Old Settler, and Enets contributions. The northernmost Turkic-speaking people.

name: Proto-Altai Turkic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Altai Turkic sub-branch (not the discredited macro-family 'Altaic'). Split into Northern Altai (Tubalar, Chelkan, Kumandy) and Southern Altai (Altai-Kizhi, Telengit, Teleut). Northern and Southern Altai are sometimes treated as separate languages with different sub-branch affiliations within Siberian Turkic.

name: Southern Altai (Altai-Kizhi)
description: Southern Altai Turkic language; the basis of the standardized literary Altai. Telengit and Teleut are sometimes treated as dialects, sometimes as separate languages.

name: Northern Altai
region: Altai Republic and Altai Krai, Russia
description: Cover term for Tubalar, Chelkan, and Kumandy — sometimes grouped with Northern Altai as a single language, sometimes treated as three separate severely endangered languages. Phonologically and lexically transitional with Yenisei Turkic (Shor, Khakas).

name: Proto-Arghu
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Arghu sub-branch, consisting of Khalaj alone. Doerfer argued for Arghu as an independent primary branch of Common Turkic, citing Khalaj retention of features otherwise lost (e.g. word-initial *h-, long vowels). Classification debated; some place Khalaj within Oghuz instead.

name: Khalaj (Khalaji)
description: Turkic language of the Khalaj people of central Iran. Documented in detail by Gerhard Doerfer, who argued it preserves features lost in all other Turkic languages including Old Turkic, making it the most conservative Turkic language in some respects. Not to be confused with the Khalaj/Khilji of Afghanistan and India (a different population).

name: Hunnic
region: Hunnic empire (steppe from Pannonia to Central Asia)
description: Putative Turkic (possibly Oghur) language of the European Hunnic confederation (c. 370–469 CE). Affiliation is among the most contested questions in steppe history: Turkic identification is challenged by Iranian, Yeniseian (Vovin), and mixed hypotheses. The link to the earlier Xiongnu is also disputed. Attested only in names and titles.

name: Proto-Finnic
region: Eastern Baltic, around the Gulf of Finland
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Finnic (Balto-Finnic) languages. Splits into Northern Finnic (Finnish, Karelian, Ingrian, Vepsian, Kven, Meänkieli) and Southern Finnic (Estonian, Võro, Livonian, Votic). Heavy Baltic and Germanic loanword strata document long Indo-European contact. The Northern/Southern split is traditional but increasingly contested.

name: Proto-Permic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Permic branch of Uralic: Komi (Zyrian, Permyak, Yazva) and Udmurt. The Permic peoples were the eastern neighbors of the Volga Finns and developed a literary tradition with the Old Permic / Abur script from the late 14th century.

name: Proto-Mordvinic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Mordvinic branch of Uralic: Erzya and Moksha. Despite being treated as dialects of a single 'Mordvin' language in 19th- and early 20th-century scholarship and in Soviet ethnographic categorization (the Mordva nationality), Erzya and Moksha are mutually unintelligible and have separate written standards.

name: Proto-Mari (Proto-Cheremis)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Mari (Cheremis) branch of Uralic. Splits into Meadow-Eastern Mari (Sornaya Mari) and Hill (Mountain) Mari (Kuryk Mari) — two mutually unintelligible literary languages.

name: Proto-Sami
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Sami languages, with a relatively recent expansion (within the last ~2000 years) from a homeland probably south of the modern Sami distribution. The pre-Sami inhabitants spoke at least one extinct non-Uralic substrate language ('Palaeo-Laplandic') detectable in toponyms, especially in Northern Sami.

name: Proto-Ugric
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Ugric branch of Uralic: Hungarian and Ob-Ugric (Khanty, Mansi). Ugric's validity as a clade is the most contested major subgrouping question in Uralic: while Hungarian shares much with Ob-Ugric, recent work (Salminen, Janhunen, Häkkinen) argues they may be sister branches separately descending from Proto-Uralic.

name: Proto-Ob-Ugric
region: Lower and middle Ob basin, western Siberia
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Ob-Ugric languages, Khanty and Mansi. Unlike the disputed Ugric grouping, the unity of Ob-Ugric is well-supported.

name: Proto-Samoyedic
region: Sayan-Altai region (probable homeland) and subsequent expansion northward
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Samoyedic branch of Uralic — the first branch to split from Proto-Uralic in the standard model. Splits into Northern Samoyedic (Nenets, Enets, Nganasan) and Southern Samoyedic (Selkup, Kamas, Mator). The homeland is generally placed in the Sayan-Altai region, with later migration into the Arctic tundra.

name: Proto-Northern Samoyedic
region: Lower Ob and Yenisei basins; subsequently the Arctic tundra
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Northern Samoyedic languages: Nenets (Tundra and Forest), Enets (Forest/Bay and Tundra), and Nganasan.

name: Proto-Southern Samoyedic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Southern Samoyedic languages: Selkup, Kamas (extinct), and Mator (extinct). The Southern Samoyedic languages preserve features lost in the Northern branch; their territorial range has contracted dramatically with Russian, Khakas, and Buryat expansion.

name: South Sami (Åarjelsaemien gïele)
description: Western Sami language; the southernmost surviving Sami language and the most divergent from the others. Phonologically and grammatically distinctive within Sami (preserves long vowels, has umlaut-like vowel alternations).

name: Ume Sami (Ubmejensámien giella)
region: Ume River basin, Sweden (and historically adjacent Norway)
description: Western Sami language; critically endangered with perhaps 10–20 fluent speakers. Recognized as an official minority language in Sweden in 2014.

name: Pite Sami (Bidumsámegiella)
description: Western Sami language; critically endangered with fewer than 50 fluent speakers.

name: Lule Sami (Julevsámegiella)
region: Lule River basin (Sweden) and adjacent Norway (Tysfjord)
description: Western Sami language; the second-largest Sami language by speakers (c. 2,000). Has a literary tradition since the 17th century.

name: Northern Sami (Davvisámegiella)
region: Finnmark and Troms (Norway), northernmost Sweden and Finland
description: Largest Sami language by speakers (c. 20,000–30,000); the de facto standard Sami in Norway, Sweden, and Finland. Has its own literary tradition, mass media (Yle Sápmi, NRK Sápmi, SVT Sápmi), and university-level instruction (Sámi University of Applied Sciences, Kautokeino). Heavy Palaeo-Laplandic substrate detected in vocabulary and toponyms.

name: Inari Sami (Anarâškielâ)
description: Eastern Sami language; the only Sami language confined to Finland. Extremely small speech community (c. 300 speakers) but the subject of an unusually successful language nest (Kielâpiervâl) revitalization program since the 1990s.

name: Skolt Sami (Sääʹmǩiõll)
region: Inari and Sevettijärvi (Finland), historically the Russian Pechenga area
description: Eastern Sami language. The Skolt Sami were largely displaced from their traditional homeland (Pechenga, Petsamo) after the 1944 Soviet annexation and resettled in Inari. Distinctive orthography using diacritics on Latin letters.

name: Akkala Sami (Áhkkilsámegiella)
region: Kola Peninsula, Russia (around the village of Yokostrov)
description: Eastern Sami language; the last known fluent speaker, Maria Sergina, died in 2003. Some descendants retain partial knowledge.

name: Kildin Sami (Кӣллт са̄мь кӣлл)
description: Eastern Sami language; the largest Sami language in Russia (c. 300–500 speakers), written in a Cyrillic-based orthography.

name: Ter Sami (Saa'mekiill)
description: Eastern Sami language; critically endangered with perhaps 2–10 elderly speakers.

name: Kemi Sami
region: Historically southern Finnish Lapland (Kuusamo, Sodankylä, Kemijärvi areas)
description: Extinct Eastern Sami language; replaced by Finnish during the 18th–19th centuries. Documented in some 17th-century missionary and naturalist materials, most famously Olaus Sirma's two yoik poems (published 1673 by Johannes Schefferus in Lapponia).

name: Ingrian (Izhorian / ižoran keeli)
description: Northern Finnic language closely related to Karelian and Finnish; critically endangered with perhaps 50–100 fluent speakers, most very elderly. The Ingrians were largely deported under Stalin in 1942.

name: Votic (Vaďďa tšeeli)
description: Southern Finnic language; the language of the Votes, one of the oldest Finnic-speaking populations of Ingria. Critically endangered with fewer than 20 speakers.

name: Livonian (līvõ kēļ)
approxDate: c. 1000–2013 CE (last L1 speaker); revitalization ongoing
region: Northern coastal Latvia (Courland coast and Livonia)
description: Southern Finnic language; the last native L1 speaker, Grizelda Kristiņa, died in 2013, but Livonian has an active L2 revitalization community. Extensive Latvian (Baltic Indo-European) contact influence — Livonian substrate is detectable in Latvian phonology and lexicon.

name: Võro (võro kiil')
description: Southern Finnic variety traditionally classified as a South Estonian dialect; increasingly recognized as a distinct language with its own literary standard and Wikipedia. Together with Seto forms the South Estonian dialect group, which is phonologically conservative within Finnic.

name: Seto (seto kiil')
region: Setomaa (southeastern Estonia and adjacent Pskov Oblast, Russia)
description: Southern Finnic variety closely related to Võro; the Seto are traditionally Orthodox Christian (in contrast to the predominantly Lutheran Estonians). Seto leelo (women's polyphonic singing tradition) was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.

name: Meänkieli (Tornedalen Finnish)
description: Northern Finnic language; classified as a dialect of Finnish until 2000, when it was recognized as one of Sweden's five official minority languages. The split from mainstream Finnish dates to the 1809 separation of Sweden and Finland and subsequent divergent development.

name: Kven (kveeni)
description: Northern Finnic language closely related to Meänkieli and dialects of Finnish; spoken by Kven communities descended from Finnish migrants to northern Norway in the 18th and 19th centuries. Recognized as a separate language in Norway in 2005.

name: Komi-Zyrian (Коми кыв)
description: Major Komi variety; the standard literary language of the Komi Republic. Direct descendant of the medieval Komi (Old Permic) tradition initiated by Stephen of Perm.

name: Komi-Permyak (Перем коми кыв)
description: Major Komi variety; the literary language of the Komi-Permyak Okrug (formerly Komi-Permyak Autonomous Okrug). Mutually intelligible to a significant degree with Komi-Zyrian, though traditionally treated as a separate language.

name: Komi-Yazva (Иньвинский язык)
description: Severely endangered Komi variety, sometimes treated as a third Komi language. Significant phonological differences from both Komi-Zyrian and Komi-Permyak.

name: Old Permic (Anbur)
description: Liturgical and literary form of Old Komi, written in the Anbur (Old Permic) script created by Stephen of Perm (Stefan Khrap, c. 1340–1396) in 1372 for the Christianization of the Komi-Zyrians. The script is a unique creation drawing on Cyrillic, Greek, and possibly Permic ritual incision marks (paj). Replaced by Cyrillic in the 17th–18th centuries.

name: Moksha (Мокшень кяль)
region: Western Mordovia and adjacent Penza Oblast, Russia
description: Major Mordvinic language; mutually unintelligible with Erzya despite the Soviet-era grouping of speakers under a single 'Mordovian' nationality. Distinctive vowel reduction system (the schwa-like /ə/ in unstressed syllables, absent in Erzya).

name: Hill Mari (Кырык мары йӹлмӹ)
region: Mari El (Volga right bank) and adjacent Nizhny Novgorod Oblast
description: Major Mari variety with its own literary standard, distinct from Meadow-Eastern Mari; mutually intelligible to only a limited degree.

name: Meadow-Eastern Mari (Олык марий йылме)
region: Mari El (Volga left bank), Bashkortostan, Tatarstan, Sverdlovsk Oblast
description: Main Mari variety with the larger literary standard; the basis of most modern Mari publishing. Eastern Mari (Bashkortostan diaspora) is sometimes treated as a third Mari literary tradition.

name: Forest Nenets
region: Forest tundra zone between Ob and Yenisei
description: Northern Samoyedic language. Forest and Tundra Nenets are mutually unintelligible and increasingly treated as separate languages rather than dialects of a single 'Nenets'.

name: Enets
region: Lower Yenisei basin, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
description: Critically endangered Northern Samoyedic language; two mutually intelligible dialects (Forest/Bay and Tundra Enets) with perhaps fewer than 50 speakers total. Heavily influenced by Nenets through long contact.

name: Nganasan
description: Northern Samoyedic language; the northernmost Uralic language. The Nganasan are descendants of the indigenous population of the Taimyr tundra who shifted to Samoyedic relatively recently (within the last few centuries). Severely endangered with perhaps a few hundred speakers.

name: Selkup
region: Yamalo-Nenets, Tyumen, Tomsk, and Krasnoyarsk regions, Russia
description: Only surviving Southern Samoyedic language; severely endangered. Three main dialect groups (Northern/Taz, Central, Southern); the Southern dialects, in particular, preserve archaic Samoyedic features lost in the more northerly varieties.

name: Kamas (Kamassian)
description: Extinct Southern Samoyedic language; the last fluent speaker, Klavdiya Plotnikova, died in 1989, having been documented extensively by Estonian linguist Ago Künnap and others in the 1960s–1980s. With Mator, formed the southern wing of Southern Samoyedic.

name: Mator (Motor)
description: Extinct Southern Samoyedic language; the language of the Mator-Taygi-Karagas group, which underwent language shift to Tofa (Sayan Turkic) and Russian by the mid-19th century. Documented primarily through 18th-century word lists collected by P. S. Pallas and others on the Russian academic expeditions.

name: Proto-Munda
region: Eastern India (homeland disputed; central or eastern India proposed)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Munda branch of Austroasiatic. Munda is unusual within the family for its highly agglutinative, suffixing typology, unlike the analytic Mon-Khmer profile. This has motivated proposals (Donegan & Stampe, Anderson) of a typological reorganization through substrate contact. Standard model: North vs. South Munda.

name: Proto-North Munda
region: Chota Nagpur plateau and adjacent central India
description: Reconstructed ancestor of North Munda, comprising the Kherwarian languages (Santali, Mundari, Ho, Bhumij, Birhor, Asuri, Turi, Korwa) and the more divergent Korku of central India.

name: Proto-Kherwarian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kherwarian subgroup of North Munda, including the largest Munda language (Santali) plus Mundari, Ho, Bhumij, Birhor, Asuri, Korwa, Turi, and others. Most Kherwarian languages are mutually intelligible to a significant degree.

name: Mundari
region: Jharkhand (especially Khunti, Ranchi, Saraikela-Kharsawan); Odisha; West Bengal; Bangladesh
description: Second-largest Munda language by speakers (~1.5 million); the language of the Munda people. Traditionally written in Devanagari, Odia, or Bengali script; the indigenous Mundari Bani / Tolong Siki script was developed by Rohidas Singh Nag in 1980.

name: Ho (Hodo Jagar)
region: Jharkhand (West Singhbhum, East Singhbhum), Odisha, Chhattisgarh
description: Major Kherwarian Munda language closely related to Mundari and Santali; the language of the Ho people. Traditionally unwritten; the indigenous Warang Citi script was developed by Lako Bodra in the 1950s and recognized in Unicode 7.0 (2014).

name: Bhumij
description: Kherwarian Munda language closely related to Mundari and Ho; sometimes treated as a Mundari dialect. The Ol Onal script was developed for Bhumij in the 1980s by Mahendra Nath Sardar.

name: Birhor
description: Kherwarian Munda language of the Birhor, a traditionally nomadic and semi-nomadic hunter-gatherer community. Severely endangered with most younger speakers shifting to Hindi or other regional languages.

name: Asuri
description: Kherwarian Munda language of the Asur, an iron-working community whose ethnonym is associated with the demonic 'Asuras' of Indo-Aryan mythology — likely reflecting pre-Aryan Munda-speaking iron technology.

name: Korwa
description: Kherwarian Munda language; subdivided into Hill Korwa and Diharu Korwa varieties.

name: Turi
description: Kherwarian Munda language; traditionally a basket-weaving community.

name: Korku
region: Southwestern Madhya Pradesh and northeastern Maharashtra (Satpura range)
description: The most geographically isolated and divergent North Munda language; the westernmost Munda language. Speakers were historically the dominant population of the Satpura range, now substantially shifted to Hindi.

name: Proto-South Munda
description: Reconstructed ancestor of South Munda, comprising the Kharia-Juang, Gutob-Remo-Gta', and Sora-Gorum-Juray subgroups. South Munda preserves more conservative Austroasiatic features than North Munda. Anderson and others argue the three subgroups are not closely related and should be separate primary branches of Munda.

name: Proto-Kharia-Juang
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Kharia and Juang, two closely related South Munda languages.

name: Kharia
region: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Assam (tea-garden communities)
description: Major South Munda language; the Kharia were dispersed in the 19th century to Assam and other tea-growing regions as plantation labor. The Hill Kharia, Delki Kharia, and Dudh Kharia subgroups are sometimes treated as separate Kharia varieties.

name: Juang
description: South Munda language closely related to Kharia; spoken by the Juang, a Scheduled Tribe in Odisha known for traditional swidden agriculture.

name: Proto-Gutob-Remo-Gta'
region: Southern Odisha and adjacent Andhra Pradesh
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Gutob-Remo-Gta' subgroup of South Munda: Gutob (Bodo Gadaba), Remo (Bonda), and Gta' (Didayi).

name: Gutob (Bodo Gadaba)
description: South Munda language of the Gadaba people of Koraput. The 'Gadaba' name applies both to this Munda-speaking community and a separate Dravidian-speaking Gadaba community (Ollari), reflecting a complex ethnic history in the area.

name: Remo (Bonda)
description: South Munda language of the Bonda (Remo) people of the Bonda Hills, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group with a distinctive material culture (the Bonda are famous for traditional bead-and-bare-torso dress).

name: Gta' (Didayi)
description: South Munda language of the Gta' (Didayi); severely endangered, perhaps 3,000 speakers. The most phonologically conservative Munda language and a key source for Proto-Munda reconstruction (Anderson).

name: Proto-Sora-Juray
region: Southern Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Sora-Juray-Gorum (Saora-Saroda) subgroup of South Munda.

name: Sora (Saora / Savara)
region: Southern Odisha (Rayagada, Gajapati) and northern Andhra Pradesh (Srikakulam)
description: Largest South Munda language; speakers are sometimes identified with the 'Savara' mentioned in classical Indian sources. The Sorang Sompeng script was developed by Mangei Gomango in 1936; recognized in Unicode 6.1 (2012).

name: Juray
description: South Munda language closely related to Sora; sometimes treated as a Sora dialect.

name: Gorum (Parengi)
description: South Munda language closely related to Sora; severely endangered.

name: Proto-Khasian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Khasian branch of Austroasiatic, the only major AA branch in northeast India (apart from Munda). Includes Khasi (Khasi-Pnar-Lyngngam dialect cluster), War, and Lyngngam. The Khasi are matrilineal; the matrilineal social organization is unusual in mainland Asia and not shared with other AA-speaking groups.

name: Pnar (Jaintia / Synteng)
description: Khasian language closely related to Khasi; the language of the Jaintia kingdom (which controlled the Jaintia Hills until annexation by the British in 1835).

name: War (War-Jaintia / War-Khasi)
description: Khasian language with significant divergence from Standard Khasi; sometimes treated as a separate language, sometimes as a Khasi dialect cluster.

name: Proto-Khmeric
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Khmer language. The Khmer branch consists of Khmer alone (with Northern Khmer/Surin Khmer as a dialect, not a separate language); historically the language of the Khmer Empire and Funan/Chenla.

name: Old Khmer (Pre-Angkorian and Angkorian Khmer)
region: Cambodia and adjacent areas (the Khmer Empire)
description: Attested ancestral form of Khmer; the language of the Khmer Empire (c. 802–1431 CE), with c. 1,200 surviving inscriptions in Old Khmer at Angkor and elsewhere. Written in a Brahmi-derived script ancestral to modern Khmer script. The transition from Old Khmer to Middle Khmer is conventionally placed in the 14th c.

name: Middle Khmer
description: Intermediate stage between Old and Modern Khmer; marked by major phonological restructuring including the development of the modern register (phonation) contrast.

name: Proto-Monic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Monic branch of Austroasiatic. Modern Monic comprises Mon (Myanmar, Thailand) and Nyahkur (central Thailand). Old Mon was a major literary and prestige language across mainland Southeast Asia (the Dvaravati and later Mon kingdoms); the Mon script is ancestral to the Burmese, Shan, and Tai scripts.

name: Old Mon
region: Dvaravati (central Thailand), Hariphunchai, and Mon kingdoms in lower Burma
description: Attested ancestral form of Mon, the literary and inscriptional language of the Dvaravati Mon kingdoms (c. 6th–11th c.) and the Mon kingdoms of lower Burma (Thaton, Pegu). Old Mon inscriptions in central Thailand are among the earliest indigenous-language inscriptions in mainland Southeast Asia. The Mon script was the source of the Burmese script.

name: Nyahkur (Niahkur)
region: Phetchabun, Chaiyaphum, Nakhon Ratchasima provinces, Thailand
description: Monic language closely related to but distinct from Mon, spoken by remnants of the Dvaravati Mon population of central Thailand that were not absorbed by Tai expansion. Severely endangered.

name: Proto-Vietic
region: Northern Vietnam, central Laos, Annamite range
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Vietic branch. Includes Viet-Muong (Vietnamese, Mường, etc.) and conservative Vietic languages (Chứt, Arem, Rục, etc.) preserving sesquisyllabic structures typical of conservative Austroasiatic. Vietnamese underwent tonogenesis through Tai and Sinitic contact, becoming a tonal, isolating language.

name: Mường
region: Hòa Bình, Thanh Hóa, Phú Thọ, Sơn La provinces, Vietnam
description: Closest living relative of Vietnamese; the language of the Mường, sometimes characterized as 'lowland Vietnamese without the Sinitic overlay'. Multiple dialects; sometimes treated as a continuum rather than one language. Significantly mutually intelligible with Vietnamese; the major Mường–Vietnamese split is dated to roughly the 10th–11th c.

name: Chứt (Rục, Sách, Arem, Mày, Mã Liềng)
region: Quảng Bình province, Vietnam; adjacent Khammouane, Laos
description: Conservative Vietic language cluster; the Chứt-speaking communities (including the Rục and Arem, who lived as cave-dwelling hunter-gatherers into the late 20th century) preserve sesquisyllabic word structures lost in Vietnamese and provide critical evidence for the pre-tonogenesis stage of Vietic.

name: Thavung (So)
region: Khammouane and Bolikhamsai, Laos; adjacent northeast Thailand
description: Conservative Vietic language of central Laos; preserves features of pre-tonal Vietic.

name: Proto-Khmuic
region: Northern Laos, adjacent Yunnan, Vietnam, Thailand
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Khmuic branch of Austroasiatic, the largest indigenous language family of northern Laos. Includes Khmu, Mlabri (Yumbri), Mal-Phrai (Thin), and Ksingmul.

name: Khmu (Kammu)
region: Northern Laos (largest indigenous population); adjacent Yunnan, Vietnam, Thailand
description: Largest Khmuic language and largest indigenous (non-Tai) language of Laos. The pre-Tai indigenous population of much of present-day Laos and northern Thailand was Khmuic-speaking; place names across the region retain Khmuic substrate. Khmu has elaborate sesquisyllabic phonology.

name: Mlabri (Yumbri)
region: Nan Province (Thailand) and adjacent northern Laos
description: Khmuic language of the Mlabri, a small foraging community ('Spirits of the Yellow Leaves' in Thai folk usage). Severely endangered, perhaps 300 speakers.

name: Proto-Palaungic
region: Eastern Burma (Shan State), western Yunnan, northern Thailand
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Palaungic (Palaung-Wa) branch of Austroasiatic. Includes Eastern Palaungic (Wa, Lawa, Bulang, Paauk) and Western Palaungic (Palaung/De'ang, Riang, Danau).

name: Wa (Vāʼ)
region: Wa State (eastern Shan State, Myanmar) and adjacent Yunnan, China
description: Largest Palaungic language; spoken across the Wa Self-Administered Division of Myanmar (effectively independent under the United Wa State Army since 1989) and adjacent Yunnan. Written in Latin and Chinese-based scripts; the historical Wa headhunting tradition was abolished in the mid-20th century.

name: Palaung (De'ang / Ta'ang)
region: Northern Shan State, Myanmar; western Yunnan, China
description: Western Palaungic language; the Ta'ang National Liberation Army has been a major armed actor in the Myanmar civil war since 2009. The De'ang ethnonym is used in China; Ta'ang and Palaung are used in Myanmar.

name: Bulang (Blang)
region: Xishuangbanna, southern Yunnan, China; adjacent Myanmar
description: Eastern Palaungic language closely related to Wa; speakers are predominantly Theravada Buddhist (an unusual feature for a Palaungic-speaking population).

name: Proto-Bahnaric
region: Central Highlands of Vietnam and adjacent Laos, Cambodia
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Bahnaric branch of Austroasiatic, the largest indigenous language family of the Central Highlands of Vietnam. Includes North Bahnaric (Bahnar, Sedang, Hre, Jeh), Central Bahnaric (Tampuan, Bunong/Mnong), South Bahnaric (Stieng, Koho, Mạ, Chrau), and West Bahnaric (Brao, Laven, Jru/Loven).

name: Bahnar (Bơhnar)
region: Gia Lai, Kon Tum, Bình Định provinces, Vietnam
description: Major North Bahnaric language; one of the first Austroasiatic languages of Vietnam to receive a Latin-based orthography (developed by French missionaries in the 19th century).

name: Sedang (Hơdrah)
region: Kon Tum province, Vietnam; adjacent Laos and Cambodia
description: North Bahnaric language famous in phonological literature for its complex vowel inventory — Sedang has been claimed to have one of the largest vowel systems in the world (Smith counts ~55 contrasting vowels).

name: Mnong (Bunong / Phnong)
region: Đắk Lắk, Đắk Nông, Lâm Đồng provinces (Vietnam) and Mondulkiri, Cambodia
description: Central Bahnaric language; the Mnong are well known for their traditional elephant-domestication culture in Mondulkiri.

name: Stieng (Xtiêng)
region: Bình Phước province, Vietnam; northeastern Cambodia
description: South Bahnaric language.

name: Brao (Lave)
description: West Bahnaric language; the Brao were historically subject to slave raids from the Lao and Khmer lowland states.

name: Proto-Katuic
region: Annamite range (central Vietnam, Laos, northeast Thailand, eastern Cambodia)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Katuic branch. Includes Katu, Pacoh, Bru, Kuy, So, Ta'oih, Ngeq, and others.

name: Katu (Kantu)
region: Central Vietnam (Quảng Nam, Thừa Thiên-Huế) and southern Laos
description: Major Katuic language; the Katu are famous for traditional wood-carving and the đâm trâu (buffalo-piercing) ritual.

name: Bru (Brou)
region: Quảng Trị (Vietnam), Savannakhet and Khammouane (Laos), northeast Thailand
description: Major Katuic language with multiple distinct varieties (Eastern Bru, Western Bru / So-Tri); often subdivided into several mutually somewhat divergent languages.

name: Kuy (Kuay / Suay)
region: Northeast Thailand, southern Laos, northern Cambodia
description: Major Katuic language; the Kuy were historically renowned as elephant catchers and mahouts for the Khmer and Thai courts.

name: Proto-Pearic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Pearic branch, the indigenous Austroasiatic languages of the Cardamom Mountains pre-dating Khmer expansion. Includes Pear, Chong, Kasong, Sa'och, Suoy, and Samre. All Pearic languages are severely endangered.

name: Chong
region: Chanthaburi and Trat provinces, Thailand; adjacent Cambodia
description: Pearic language; the largest Pearic language by speakers but still severely endangered (a few thousand speakers). Notable for preserving a four-way register/phonation contrast unusual within Austroasiatic.

name: Proto-Aslian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Aslian branch of Austroasiatic, the indigenous languages of the Orang Asli of the Malay Peninsula. Includes Northern Aslian (Jahaic: Kensiu, Jahai, Batek; Maniq in Thailand), Central Aslian (Senoic: Semai, Temiar, Lanoh, Jah Hut), and Southern Aslian (Semelai, Semaq Beri, Temoq, Mah Meri).

name: Semai
description: Largest Aslian language; one of the few Austroasiatic languages of the Malay Peninsula to maintain a vigorous speech community. The Semai have been frequently cited in anthropology (e.g. Robert Knox Dentan) for traditionally low levels of interpersonal violence.

name: Temiar
description: Central Aslian (Senoic) language; documented extensively by Geoffrey Benjamin.

name: Jahai
region: Perak and Kelantan, Malaysia; adjacent southern Thailand
description: Northern Aslian (Jahaic) language. Famous in linguistic anthropology and cognitive science for its elaborate olfactory vocabulary — Jahai speakers, like several other Aslian-speaking peoples, name smells using a system of dedicated abstract terms (rather than source-based descriptions as in most European languages).

name: Proto-Nicobarese
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Nicobarese branch of Austroasiatic, indigenous to the Nicobar Islands. Includes Car Nicobarese (most widely spoken), Chowra, Teressa, Central, Southern Nicobarese, and Shompen (whose Austroasiatic affiliation is disputed). The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami devastated the Nicobarese-speaking population.

name: Car Nicobarese
description: Largest Nicobarese language; the language of Car Nicobar Island. Written in Latin script; widely Christian since 19th–20th c. missionary activity.

name: Shompen (Shom Peng)
description: Language of the Shompen, an isolated indigenous community in the interior of Great Nicobar; classification within Nicobarese has been disputed (some treat Shompen as an isolate or as having only an areal relationship to Nicobarese). Critically endangered, perhaps 200 speakers; the Shompen avoid contact with outsiders.

name: Proto-Khoe-Kwadi
region: Southern Africa (and possibly East Africa, per the pastoralist-migration hypothesis)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Khoe-Kwadi family, the largest and most securely established southern African 'Khoisan' family. Comprises the Khoe branch (Khoekhoe and Kalahari Khoe) and the extinct Kwadi of Angola. Güldemann links it to an immigrant pre-Bantu pastoralist population, distinct from the indigenous Kxʼa and Tuu forager speakers.

name: Kwadi
description: Extinct sister of the entire Khoe branch within Khoe-Kwadi; the language of a cattle-herding people of southwestern Angola. Documented only fragmentarily (mid-20th-century fieldwork by António de Almeida and others) before its extinction. Its position as sister to Khoe is the basis for the 'Khoe-Kwadi' family name.

name: Proto-Khoe
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Khoe branch of Khoe-Kwadi, divided into Khoekhoe (Khoekhoe proper, Nama-Damara, ǂAakhoe, Haiǁom, and the extinct Cape varieties such as ǃOra/Korana and Xiri/Griqua) and Kalahari Khoe (East: Shua, Tshwa; West: Khwe, Naro, Gǁana, Gǀui, Ts'ixa).

name: Nama (Khoekhoegowab / Damara-Nama)
region: Namibia, southwestern Botswana, Northern Cape (South Africa)
description: Largest 'Khoisan' language by far (c. 200,000+ speakers), spoken by the Nama and Damara peoples. The only southern African click language with national-language status (in Namibia) and substantial institutional support, education materials, and media. Standard orthography uses Latin letters plus four click symbols (ǀ ǁ ǂ ǃ).

name: Korana (ǃOra)
description: Effectively extinct Khoekhoe language of the Korana people; the last fluent speakers were recorded in the late 20th century. Together with Xiri represents the Cape Khoekhoe varieties that were the first southern African languages encountered and recorded by European colonists at the Cape (17th c.).

name: Xiri (Griqua)
region: Northern Cape and Free State, South Africa
description: Moribund/extinct Khoekhoe language of the Griqua people (a partly creole-origin Khoe community of the 18th–19th-century Cape frontier). A handful of elderly semi-speakers reported in the early 21st century.

name: Haiǁom
description: Khoekhoe language; the Haiǁom are a formerly forager people who shifted to a Khoekhoe (Nama-like) language, in contrast to most foragers of the region who spoke Kxʼa or Tuu languages. The Haiǁom were evicted from Etosha National Park in the 1950s, a major land-rights grievance.

name: Naro (Nharo)
region: Ghanzi District, western Botswana; adjacent Namibia
description: West Kalahari Khoe language; one of the better-documented Kalahari Khoe languages, with a Latin-based orthography (developed by the Naro Language Project) and Bible translation work. The Naro are a San people of the Ghanzi farming district.

name: Gǀui (Gǁana-Gǀui)
description: West Kalahari Khoe language closely related to Gǁana; spoken by San communities of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve, who were controversially relocated by the Botswana government from the 1990s. Gǀui has one of the largest consonant inventories in the world, including a rich click system.

name: Gǁana
description: West Kalahari Khoe language closely related to Gǀui; sometimes treated as a single Gǀui-Gǁana language.

name: Khwe (Kxoe)
region: Caprivi Strip (Namibia), northwestern Botswana, southwestern Zambia, Angola
description: West Kalahari Khoe language; many Khwe were displaced and militarized during the Angolan and Namibian conflicts of the late 20th century. Now substantially refugee/resettled communities.

name: Ts'ixa
description: Small West Kalahari Khoe variety, documentation of which (Andrason, Fehn and others) has clarified Kalahari Khoe subgrouping. Endangered.

name: Shua
description: East Kalahari Khoe language cluster (Deti, Cara, Tshwao, etc.).

name: Tshwa (Kua)
description: East Kalahari Khoe language cluster.

name: Proto-Kxʼa
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kxʼa family, shown by Heine & Honken (2010) to unite the Juu (ǃXuun/Juǀʼhoan) dialect cluster with the small ǂʼAmkoe of Botswana. One of the three established southern African click families. Juu and Tuu are associated with indigenous forager (San) populations, unlike the immigrant pastoralist Khoe-Kwadi.

name: Proto-Juu (Proto-Juu-ǃXuun)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Juu (Ju, ǃKung) dialect cluster, a chain of varieties stretching across northern Namibia, northwestern Botswana, and southern Angola. Includes Northwestern (ǃKung/ǃXuun), Southeastern (Juǀʼhoan), and Central varieties.

name: Juǀʼhoan (Southeastern ǃKung)
region: Northeastern Namibia (Nyae Nyae) and northwestern Botswana
description: Best-documented Kxʼa language; the variety on which most linguistic, anthropological (the Harvard Kalahari Project), and orthographic work has focused. Juǀʼhoan has one of the largest phonemic inventories of any language, with dozens of click phonemes. The Nyae Nyae Conservancy is a notable community-based land and language initiative.

name: ǃXuun (Northwestern ǃKung / Ekoka ǃKung)
description: Northwestern Juu dialect cluster; many speakers were displaced into Namibia and South Africa during the Angolan civil war. A community of ǃXuun speakers (with Khwe) was resettled at Platfontein, South Africa, after service with the South African Defence Force.

name: ǂʼAmkoe (ǂHoan)
description: Critically endangered Kxʼa language (perhaps a few dozen elderly speakers), the sister of the entire Juu cluster within Kxʼa. Its demonstrated relationship to Juu (Heine & Honken 2010) established the Kxʼa family. Three divergent dialects (Sasi, ǂHoan, Nǃaqriaxe).

name: Proto-Tuu (Proto-Taa-ǃKwi)
region: Southern Kalahari and South African interior
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tuu (Taa-ǃKwi, formerly 'Southern Khoisan') family. Comprises the Taa branch (ǃXóõ) and the ǃKwi branch (Nǁng, ǀXam, ǁXegwi, etc.). The ǃKwi languages belonged to the San of the South African interior, most killed during colonial expansion; Tuu is now reduced to ǃXóõ (endangered) and Nǁng (nearly extinct).

name: Taa (ǃXóõ)
description: The principal surviving Tuu language; famous for the largest phoneme inventory of any documented language — depending on analysis, 80 to 160+ consonants, including five basic click types with many accompaniments, plus a large vowel system with phonation contrasts. Documented in detail by Anthony Traill. Endangered, with a few thousand speakers.

name: Nǁng (Nǀuu / ǂKhomani)
region: Northern Cape (around the Kalahari Gemsbok / ǃXaus), South Africa
description: Critically endangered ǃKwi (ǃUi) Tuu language; the last fluent speakers (notably Katrina Esau, who has run community teaching efforts) numbered only a handful in the 2010s. The ǂKhomani San land claim in the Northern Cape (settled 1999) is a landmark South African indigenous land-rights case. Closely related to the extinct ǀXam.

name: ǀXam
description: Extinct ǃKwi Tuu language extensively documented in the 1870s by Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd, whose archive of ǀXam narratives and mythology is one of the richest records of any extinct language and a UNESCO Memory of the World collection. The South African national motto is in ǀXam. Speakers were largely killed or assimilated under colonialism.

name: ǁXegwi
region: Southeastern Transvaal / Mpumalanga (around Lake Chrissie), South Africa
description: Extinct ǃKwi Tuu language; the easternmost Tuu language, spoken in an area otherwise dominated by Bantu languages. The last speaker is reported to have died in the late 20th century.

name: Proto-Gunwinyguan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Gunwinyguan family, the largest non-Pama-Nyungan family, centered on Arnhem Land. Includes Bininj Kunwok, Dalabon, Rembarrnga, Ngalakgan, Ngandi, Jawoyn, and Kunbarlang. Highly polysynthetic. Its reconstruction (Alpher, Evans, Harvey) is one of the few well-developed for a non-Pama-Nyungan family.

name: Bininj Kunwok (Gunwinggu / Kunwinjku)
description: Largest Gunwinyguan language and one of the strongest non-Pama-Nyungan languages, with several thousand speakers across mutually intelligible dialects (Kunwinjku, Kuninjku, Kundjeyhmi, Mayali). Highly polysynthetic; a single verb can express a complete clause. Robust intergenerational transmission, unusual among Australian languages.

name: Dalabon (Dangbon / Ngalkbun)
description: Gunwinyguan language; severely endangered. Documented extensively (Evans, Merlan, Ponsonnet); noted for an elaborate system of emotion and 'tri-relational' kinship vocabulary.

name: Rembarrnga
description: Gunwinyguan language; polysynthetic with prefixing verb morphology.

name: Ngalakgan
region: Roper River region, southeastern Arnhem Land, NT
description: Gunwinyguan language; nearly extinct. Documented by Merlan and Baker.

name: Jawoyn
description: Gunwinyguan language of the Jawoyn people, traditional owners of Nitmiluk (Katherine Gorge) and parts of Kakadu. Severely endangered.

name: Kunbarlang
description: Gunwinyguan language closely associated with Bininj Kunwok-speaking communities; endangered.

name: Proto-Worrorran
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Worrorran family of the northern Kimberley. Three branches: Worrorric (Worrorra, Unggumi), Wunambalic (Wunambal, Gambera), and Ngarinyinic (Ngarinyin/Ungarinyin). Associated with the Wandjina rock-art tradition of the Kimberley. Worrorran languages have unusual multiple noun-class (gender) systems.

name: Ngarinyin (Ungarinyin)
description: Largest Worrorran language; the Ngarinyin are custodians of major Wandjina and Gwion Gwion (Bradshaw) rock-art sites. Severely endangered.

name: Worrorra
description: Worrorran language; nearly extinct.

name: Wunambal (Gaambera)
description: Worrorran language; critically endangered.

name: Proto-Nyulnyulan
region: Dampier Peninsula and west Kimberley, WA
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Nyulnyulan family of the western Kimberley. Two branches: Western Nyulnyulan (Nyulnyul, Bardi, Jawi, Jabirrjabirr, Nimanburru) and Eastern Nyulnyulan (Nyikina, Warrwa, Yawuru). Among the few non-Pama-Nyungan families with a published comparative reconstruction (Stokes & McGregor).

name: Bardi
region: Northern Dampier Peninsula and islands, WA
description: Best-documented Nyulnyulan language (Bowern, Metcalfe); endangered but with active documentation and revitalization.

name: Yawuru
description: Eastern Nyulnyulan language; subject of active community revitalization in Broome (Mabu Yawuru ngan-ga).

name: Nyikina
description: Eastern Nyulnyulan language; severely endangered.

name: Proto-Bunuban
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the small Bunuban family, comprising Bunuba and Gooniyandi. Bunuban languages are notable for complex verb structures with coverbs.

name: Bunuba (Bunaba)
description: Bunuban language; associated with the resistance leader Jandamarra (1870s–1897). Severely endangered.

name: Gooniyandi
description: Bunuban language documented by McGregor; severely endangered.

name: Proto-Jarrakan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Jarrakan (Djeragan) family of the east Kimberley: Kija, Miriwoong, Gajirrabeng, Gija. Multiple noun-class systems.

name: Kija (Gija)
description: Jarrakan language; the Warmun community is famous for the Gija ochre-painting movement (Rover Thomas and others). Endangered.

name: Miriwoong (Miriuwung)
region: Kununurra region, east Kimberley, WA / NT
description: Jarrakan language; critically endangered but with active work at the Mirima Dawang Woorlab-gerring language centre in Kununurra.

name: Proto-Western Daly
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Western Daly family (Marranj/Marringarr, Marri Tjevin, Marri Ammu, Magati Ke). One of several distinct, not-demonstrably-related families in the Daly River region of the NT — the Daly is a major locus of non-Pama-Nyungan linguistic diversity.

name: Marranj (Marringarr)
description: Western Daly language; severely endangered.

name: Proto-Southern Daly
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Southern Daly family, comprising Murrinh-Patha and Ngan'gityemerri (Ngan'gi). The unity of Southern Daly has been questioned; the two languages are quite divergent.

name: Murrinh-Patha
description: One of the very few Australian Aboriginal languages with a growing speaker base and robust child transmission, owing to its role as the lingua franca of the large Wadeye community. Extremely polysynthetic, with a complex 'bipartite' verb structure and numeral/classifier systems that have attracted much typological attention (Walsh, Nordlinger).

name: Ngan'gityemerri (Ngan'gi)
description: Southern Daly language documented by Reid; severely endangered.

name: Malak-Malak (Mullukmulluk)
description: Northern Daly language (the Northern Daly 'family' may be only Malak-Malak and the closely related Matngele); critically endangered.

name: Proto-Iwaidjan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Iwaidjan family of the Cobourg Peninsula region: Iwaidja, Mawng (Maung), Amurdak, Ilgar, Garig. Iwaidjan languages have unusual verb morphology and (in Iwaidja) a striking system of 'kinship verbs'.

name: Iwaidja
region: Croker Island and Cobourg Peninsula, NT
