description: Iwaidjan language; severely endangered. Famous for verbs that encode kinship relations between participants (e.g. a verb meaning 'to have as a mother's brother').

name: Mawng (Maung)
description: Iwaidjan language; one of the stronger Iwaidjan languages, with continuing use at Warruwi.

name: Amurdak (Amarag)
description: Iwaidjan language; critically endangered, very few speakers.

name: Proto-Tangkic
region: Southern Gulf of Carpentaria, Wellesley Islands, Qld/NT
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tangkic family of the southern Gulf of Carpentaria (Wellesley Islands and adjacent mainland): Lardil, Kayardild, Yangkaal, Yukulta, Nguburindi, and Minkin (the last extinct and poorly attested). Tangkic is sometimes argued to be more closely related to Pama-Nyungan than other NPN families, but this is unresolved.

name: Kayardild
region: Bentinck and Sweers Islands, Gulf of Carpentaria, Qld
description: Tangkic language famous in linguistic typology for 'verbal case' and extreme 'case stacking' (multiple layered case suffixes encoding modal and temporal as well as relational information), documented by Nicholas Evans. Critically endangered; speakers were relocated from Bentinck Island to Mornington Island in 1948.

name: Lardil (Leerdil)
region: Mornington Island, Gulf of Carpentaria, Qld
description: Tangkic language; famous for Damin, an auxiliary initiation register (a 'ceremonial language' with phonemes — including click-like ingressives — found in no ordinary Australian language) used by initiated men. Lardil proper is critically endangered.

name: Mangarrayi
description: Non-Pama-Nyungan language sometimes grouped with the Maran languages (Alawa, Marra, Warndarrang) into a 'Mangarrayi-Maran' family, though this grouping is uncertain. Critically endangered.

name: Marra (Mara)
region: Limmen Bight / Roper region, southeastern Arnhem Land, NT
description: Maran non-Pama-Nyungan language; critically endangered. Highly polysynthetic with prefixing morphology and noun classes.

name: Alawa
description: Maran non-Pama-Nyungan language; critically endangered.

name: Garrwa (Garawa)
region: Southern Gulf of Carpentaria, NT/Qld border
description: Garrwan non-Pama-Nyungan language (with Wanyi); one of the relatively stronger NPN languages of the southern Gulf, with continuing use at Borroloola and Robinson River.

name: Wambaya
description: West Barkly language of the Mirndi family (a geographically split NPN family with a western Victoria River branch and an eastern Barkly branch — Wambaya, Gudanji, Binbinka, Jingulu). Wambaya is famous for radically free word order with second-position clitic clusters carrying agreement (Nordlinger). Critically endangered.

name: Jingulu (Djingili)
description: Eastern Mirndi language; noted for verb structure in which only a handful of true verb roots combine with many coverbs (Pensalfini). Critically endangered.

name: Jaminjung (Djamindjung)
description: Western Mirndi (Yirram) language; the geographic split between western Mirndi (Victoria River) and eastern Mirndi (Barkly) is one of the more striking discontinuous NPN distributions. Critically endangered.

name: Giimbiyu (Mengerrdji-Urningangk-Erre)
region: Western Arnhem Land (East Alligator region), NT
description: Essentially extinct small Giimbiyu family of western Arnhem Land (Mengerrdji, Urningangk, Erre), distinct from neighbouring Gunwinyguan and Iwaidjan. Among the most poorly documented Australian families.

name: Anindilyakwa (Enindhilyakwa)
region: Groote Eylandt, Gulf of Carpentaria, NT
description: Highly polysynthetic non-Pama-Nyungan language of Groote Eylandt, often classified as an isolate though sometimes linked to Gunwinyguan. One of the few Australian languages with robust transmission. Famous for extreme morphological complexity, an elaborate noun-class system, and a traditional base-5/base-20 numeral system.

name: Wagiman (Wageman)
region: Daly River / Pine Creek region, NT
description: Non-Pama-Nyungan isolate of the upper Daly region; critically endangered. Notable for a small closed class of inflecting verbs combined with coverbs.

name: Umbugarla
description: Non-Pama-Nyungan isolate; effectively extinct (one or two rememberers documented in the late 20th century).

name: Ngurmbur
region: Arnhem Land fringe / Daly region, NT
description: Very poorly attested, essentially extinct non-Pama-Nyungan language of uncertain affiliation.

name: Krio
description: English-lexifier creole; native language of the Sierra Leone Krio people (descendants of freed African Americans, Jamaican Maroons, and 'Liberated Africans' resettled at Freetown from the 1790s) and a lingua franca of Sierra Leone. Substantial Yoruba and West African substrate. Closely related to Nigerian Pidgin and the Atlantic English creoles.

name: Liberian Kreyol (Liberian English / Kolokwa)
description: English-lexifier creole continuum of Liberia, influenced by the speech of Settler (Americo-Liberian) communities of African American origin as well as indigenous languages. Ranges from acrolectal Liberian Settler English to basilectal Kolokwa (Liberian Pidgin English).

name: Nigerian Pidgin (Naijá)
description: English-lexifier creole/expanded pidgin; with tens of millions of speakers (L1 for some, L2 for many), one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa. Increasingly used in broadcasting (e.g. BBC News Pidgin, launched 2017). Heavy substrate from Edo, Yoruba, Igbo, and others. The status of Naijá as creole vs. expanded pidgin is debated.

name: Cameroon Pidgin English (Kamtok)
description: English-lexifier creole/expanded pidgin of Cameroon; a major lingua franca, especially in the Anglophone (Northwest and Southwest) regions. Closely related to Nigerian Pidgin and Krio.

name: Ghanaian Pidgin English
description: English-lexifier pidgin/creole of Ghana, with a notable 'student pidgin' variety used among (especially male) secondary and tertiary students. Part of the West African English-creole continuum.

name: Gullah (Geechee / Sea Island Creole)
region: Sea Islands and Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia, USA
description: English-lexifier creole of the Gullah/Geechee people, descendants of enslaved Africans on the rice and indigo plantations of the southeastern US coast. The only English creole indigenous to the continental US. Strong West/Central African substrate (Kongo, Mende, Vai, Twi); long studied for its African retentions. Related to Caribbean creoles.

name: Bajan (Barbadian Creole)
description: English-lexifier creole of Barbados; relatively acrolectal (close to English) compared with other Caribbean creoles, owing to Barbados's plantation-society history. Mesolectal continuum with Barbadian Standard English.

name: Trinidadian Creole (Trini)
description: English-lexifier creole of Trinidad; substrate and adstrate influence from French Creole (the earlier prestige creole of Trinidad), Bhojpuri (Indo-Trinidadian indentured-labour community), Spanish, and African languages. Tobagonian Creole is a related but distinct variety.

name: Guyanese Creole (Creolese)
description: English-lexifier creole of Guyana; classic locus of the 'creole continuum' (basilect–mesolect–acrolect) model developed by Derek Bickerton on Guyanese data. Substantial Bhojpuri and African substrate.

name: Belizean Creole (Kriol)
description: English-lexifier creole of Belize, the lingua franca of the country across ethnic lines. Closely related to Jamaican and Miskito Coast Creole.

name: Sranan Tongo
description: English-lexifier creole of Suriname (despite the territory's later Dutch colonial rule), the lingua franca of the country. Among the most-studied creoles. Related deeply to the Surinamese Maroon creoles (Saramaccan, Ndyuka), which preserve especially archaic English- and Portuguese-derived strata.

name: Saramaccan
description: English-lexifier (with heavy Portuguese admixture) Maroon creole of the Saramaka, descendants of self-liberated enslaved Africans who formed independent communities in the Surinamese interior. Famous for a phonemic tone system (from its African substrate) and its dual English/Portuguese lexical base. Often cited in creole-simplicity debates.

name: Ndyuka (Aukan)
region: Eastern interior Suriname and French Guiana (Ndyuka Maroons)
description: English-lexifier Maroon creole of the Ndyuka (Aukan) people. Written in the indigenous Afaka syllabary, created c. 1910 by Afáka Atumisi — one of very few scripts invented for a creole language.

name: Mauritian Creole (Kreol Morisien)
description: French-lexifier creole; the most widely spoken language of Mauritius and a strong L1 across ethnic lines. Part of the Indian Ocean (Bourbonnais) French-creole group. Substrate from East African, Malagasy, and (later) Bhojpuri languages of the enslaved and indentured populations. Increasingly standardized in writing (Lortograf Kreol Morisien).

name: Réunion Creole (Kréol Rénioné)
description: French-lexifier creole of Réunion; structurally closer to French than Mauritian or Seychellois (more acrolectal/less restructured), the subject of debate over whether it is a 'creole' in the same sense. Part of the Indian Ocean French-creole group.

name: Seychellois Creole (Seselwa / Kreol)
description: French-lexifier creole; one of the three official languages of Seychelles (with English and French) and the first language of nearly the entire population. Has official orthography and standardization (Lenstiti Kreol). Indian Ocean French-creole group.

name: Louisiana Creole (Kouri-Vini)
description: French-lexifier creole of Louisiana, distinct from Louisiana Regional (Cajun) French. Severely endangered, with active revitalization (the autonym 'Kouri-Vini' has been promoted to distinguish it from Cajun French). African (notably Bambara/Mande, Fon) substrate.

name: Antillean Creole (Kréyòl)
region: Lesser Antilles (Martinique, Guadeloupe, Dominica, St. Lucia)
description: French-lexifier creole continuum of the Lesser Antilles, with regional varieties (Martinican, Guadeloupean, Dominican, Saint Lucian). Closely related to Haitian Creole within the broader Caribbean French-creole group. Vehicle of a major francophone Creole literary and theoretical movement (créolité; Glissant, Chamoiseau, Confiant).

name: French Guianese Creole (Kriyòl gwiyannen)
description: French-lexifier creole of French Guiana; related to Antillean Creole but with distinct features and Portuguese, English, and Amerindian influence.

name: Tayo (Saint-Louis Creole)
description: French-lexifier creole of New Caledonia, with Melanesian (Kanak, especially Drehu and the Houaïlou-area languages) substrate. One of very few French creoles in the Pacific; emerged in a 19th-century Catholic mission community.

name: Cape Verdean Creole (Kabuverdianu / Kriolu)
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole; the oldest documented surviving creole (Cape Verde settled from the 1460s) and the most widely spoken Portuguese creole. The L1 of nearly all Cape Verdeans, with two main dialect groups (Sotavento; Barlavento). Part of the Upper Guinea Portuguese-creole group. Large diaspora. ALUPEC standard orthography.

name: Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriol)
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole; the lingua franca of Guinea-Bissau across its many ethnolinguistic groups. Part of the Upper Guinea group with Cape Verdean Creole; substrate from Mande and Atlantic (Manjak, Balanta, etc.) languages.

name: Kristang (Papiá Kristang / Malacca Creole)
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of the Malacca Portuguese-Eurasian community, descended from the Portuguese capture of Malacca (1511). Malay and Hokkien substrate/adstrate. Critically endangered, with revitalization efforts (e.g. the Kodrah Kristang initiative in Singapore).

name: Macanese (Patuá / Maquista)
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of the Macanese (Eurasian) community of Macau, with Cantonese, Malay, and Sinhala/Indo-Portuguese influences. Critically endangered (a few dozen elderly speakers), maintained partly through theatre (teatro patuá).

name: Korlai Portuguese (Kristi)
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of an isolated Indo-Portuguese Catholic community south of Mumbai, with Marathi substrate. Documented in detail by J. Clancy Clements; endangered.

name: Sri Lankan Portuguese Creole
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of the Burgher and Portuguese Mechanic communities of Sri Lanka, with Tamil and Sinhala substrate. Notable for having acquired typologically 'Indic' features (e.g. SOV order, case marking) through long contact. Severely endangered.

name: Angolar (N'gola)
region: São Tomé (southern part), São Tomé and Príncipe
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of the Angolares, traditionally a fishing community of São Tomé reputedly descended in part from survivors of a slave-ship wreck and from Maroons. Part of the Gulf of Guinea Portuguese-creole group; especially heavy Kimbundu/Kikongo (Bantu) substrate.

name: Forro (Santome / São-Toméan Creole)
region: São Tomé, São Tomé and Príncipe
description: Portuguese-lexifier creole of São Tomé; the main creole of the island, descended from the late-15th/16th-century plantation society. Gulf of Guinea group, with Edo and Kongo/Kimbundu substrate.

name: Chavacano (Chabacano)
region: Zamboanga, Cavite, and other areas of the Philippines
description: The only Spanish-lexifier creole in Asia and the most-spoken Spanish creole overall; the principal variety is Zamboangueño (Chavacano de Zamboanga). Tagalog, Cebuano, Hiligaynon, and other Philippine substrate, with Spanish-derived lexicon. Multiple regional varieties (Zamboangueño, Caviteño, Ternateño, etc.).

name: Palenquero (Lengua)
description: Spanish-lexifier creole of San Basilio de Palenque, a town founded by self-liberated enslaved Africans (cimarrones) southeast of Cartagena — often called the first free African town in the Americas. Strong Kikongo/Kimbundu (Bantu) substrate. UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity (2005). Endangered but reviving.

name: Juba Arabic
description: Arabic-lexifier creole/pidgin of South Sudan; a major lingua franca, especially in the south. Emerged from the contact Arabic of 19th-century Egyptian-Sudanese military camps and trade (the 'Bimbashi Arabic' of the Turco-Egyptian and Mahdist periods). Substrate from Bari and other Nilotic and Central Sudanic languages. Related to Nubi.

name: Nubi (Ki-Nubi)
region: Uganda and Kenya (Nubi communities, e.g. Bombo, Kibera)
description: Arabic-lexifier creole spoken by the Nubi, descendants of 19th-century Sudanese (Equatorial) soldiers (the 'Emin Pasha' troops) resettled in East Africa under British colonial service. Closely related to Juba Arabic but with greater Swahili and Bantu influence and full creolization (it is an L1 community language). Notable for tonal features.

name: Negerhollands
region: US Virgin Islands (formerly Danish West Indies: St. Thomas, St. John)
description: Extinct Dutch-lexifier creole of the former Danish West Indies; the last known speaker, Alice Stevenson, died in 1987. Extensively documented from the 18th century onward (Moravian and Danish missionaries produced religious texts and grammars), making it one of the best-attested historical creoles.

name: Berbice Dutch
description: Extinct Dutch-lexifier creole notable for an unusually identifiable single African substrate — Eastern Ijo (Kalabari), reflecting a concentrated origin of the enslaved population. The last fluent speakers were recorded around the 1990s–2000s (Ian Robertson, Silvia Kouwenberg). A key case in creole-genesis substrate research.

name: Skepi Dutch
description: Poorly attested, extinct Dutch-lexifier creole of the Essequibo (Skepi) region of Guyana; known mainly from a small amount of recorded material.

name: Baba Malay
description: Malay-lexifier creole of the Peranakan (Straits Chinese / Baba-Nyonya) community, with Hokkien substrate. The language of a distinctive Sino-Malay culture; endangered.

name: Betawi (Batavian Malay)
description: Malay-lexifier creole that emerged among the ethnically mixed population of colonial Batavia; the language of the Betawi people of Jakarta. Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese (Hokkien), Balinese, and other substrate/adstrate. (Note: 'malay' lexifier node assumed present in dataset.)

name: Russenorsk
region: Arctic coast (northern Norway, Kola Peninsula / Pomor trade)
description: Extinct Russian–Norwegian trade pidgin of the Pomor trade between Russian merchants and northern Norwegian fishermen. Famous in pidgin/creole linguistics as a near-textbook 'dual-source' pidgin with a roughly balanced Russian/Norwegian lexicon and minimal, symmetrical grammar; died out after the Russian Revolution ended the Pomor trade.

name: Chinook Jargon (Chinuk Wawa)
region: Pacific Northwest (Oregon, Washington, British Columbia, Alaska)
description: Trade pidgin of the Pacific Northwest based primarily on Lower Chinookan and Nuu-chah-nulth, with later French and English additions via the fur trade. Reached perhaps 100,000+ users at its 19th-century peak. Creolized in some communities, notably Grand Ronde in Oregon, where Chinuk Wawa is now taught and revitalized as a heritage language.

name: Lingua Franca (Sabir / Mediterranean Lingua Franca)
description: The original 'Lingua Franca' — a Romance-lexifier (Italian, Occitan/Spanish, later French) contact pidgin of the medieval and early-modern Mediterranean, used among European, Arab, Turkish, and Berber traders and captives. The source of the generic term 'lingua franca'. Attested fragmentarily; an 1830 dictionary records a late Algiers form.

name: Hudson Strait / Eskimo Trade Jargon
description: Extinct Inuit–European (and Inuit–Amerindian) trade jargons of the eastern Arctic, including Hudson Strait Trade Jargon. Poorly attested. (Lexifier node 'inuktitut' assumed present; if absent, see note.)

name: Hiri Motu (Police Motu)
description: Pidginized form of Motu (an Austronesian Oceanic language), originally based on the hiri trade-voyage contact speech of the Motu and elaborated as 'Police Motu' under the colonial constabulary. One of the official languages of Papua New Guinea, though now declining relative to Tok Pisin and English. (Parented to Motu.)

name: Michif
region: Métis communities of the northern Plains (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, North Dakota)
description: Mixed language of the Métis, combining French-origin noun phrases (French gender, articles, adjectives) and Cree-origin verb phrases and verbal morphology. A canonical example of a mixed language that is not a creole: it shows full grammatical complexity from both sources rather than creole-type simplification. Endangered. Sources: Cree and French.

name: Media Lengua
description: Mixed language with Spanish-derived lexical roots inserted into Quichua (Ecuadorian Quechua) grammatical structure ('relexification'); a textbook case in the mixed-language literature (Pieter Muysken). Spoken in a few highland Ecuadorian communities. (Parented to Quechua as the grammatical-frame source.)

name: Mednyj Aleut (Copper Island Aleut)
region: Copper Island (Bering Island area), Commander Islands, Russia
description: Mixed language combining Aleut nominal and lexical material with Russian finite-verb morphology — an unusual 'intertwined' language splitting the verb between two sources. Critically endangered/moribund. Arose in the mixed Russian-Aleut Creole (Creole-class) community of the Commander Islands. (Parented to Aleut.)

name: Ma'a / Mbugu
description: Mixed language with a Cushitic-derived lexical stratum embedded in a Bantu (Pare/Shambaa-like) grammatical structure; speakers shift between a normal Bantu register (Normal Mbugu) and the special Ma'a vocabulary. A key case in debates over language mixing and 'para-lexification' (Mous). The Bantu grammatical source is Pare.

name: Light Warlpiri
description: A newly emerged mixed language (documented by Carmel O'Shannessy) combining Warlpiri nominal morphology with a verbal system drawn largely from English and Kriol, plus an innovative auxiliary system. Notable as one of the few mixed languages whose genesis was observed essentially in real time, among children at Lajamanu from the 1980s.

name: Gurindji Kriol
region: Kalkaringi and Daguragu, Northern Territory, Australia
description: Mixed language combining Gurindji (Pama-Nyungan) nominal morphology with Kriol verbal structure, documented by Felicity Meakins and Patrick McConvell. Like Light Warlpiri, a recently-formed mixed language emerging from a shift situation. (Parented to Gurindji; if 'gurindji' absent, parented to proto-pama-nyungan.)

name: Proto-Aztecan (Proto-Nahuan-Pochutec)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Aztecan (Nahuan) branch of Uto-Aztecan, the southernmost group. Splits into General Aztec (the Nahuatl dialect complex) and the divergent, now-extinct Pochutec of coastal Oaxaca. The southward spread of Nahuan into central Mexico is associated with movements culminating in the Nahua peoples (the Mexica/Aztec).

name: Proto-Nahuan (Proto-Nahuatl / General Aztec)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Nahuatl dialect complex (General Aztec, excluding Pochutec). Diversified into Eastern and Western (and Central) dialect groups; the *-tl / *-t / *-tla reflex of the absolutive suffix is a classic isogloss dividing the modern dialects.

name: Colonial Nahuatl
description: Nahuatl written in the Latin alphabet through the Spanish colonial period — by far the largest indigenous-language documentary corpus of the Americas (the basis of the 'New Philology': wills, land records, annals). Classical Nahuatl is the prestige early-colonial form; later colonial Nahuatl shows growing Spanish influence.

name: Pipil (Nawat)
description: Southernmost Nahuan language, the result of a pre-Columbian Nahua migration into Central America. Severely endangered/moribund (its decline accelerated after the 1932 Salvadoran matanza, when speaking it became dangerous); active revitalization since the 2000s. Sometimes classified as a divergent dialect of Nahuatl, sometimes a separate language.

name: Proto-Eastern Mayan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Eastern Mayan, comprising the Quichean (K'iche', Kaqchikel, Tz'utujil, Q'eqchi', Poqomam, Poqomchi', etc.) and Mamean (Mam, Awakatek, Ixil, Tektitek) subgroups.

name: Proto-Quichean (Proto-K'ichean)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Quichean subgroup of Eastern Mayan. The Popol Vuh — the K'iche' council-book of mythology and dynastic history — is the most famous literary work of any Mesoamerican language.

name: Colonial K'iche'
description: The form of K'iche' written in the Latin alphabet during the Spanish colonial period; the language of the surviving manuscript of the Popol Vuh (copied/transcribed by Francisco Ximénez c. 1701–1703 from an earlier alphabetic original) and of the Título de Totonicapán, the Rabinal Achí dance-drama, and other early documents.

name: Proto-Mamean
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Mamean subgroup of Eastern Mayan: Mam, Tektitek, Awakatek, Ixil.

name: Proto-Yucatecan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Yucatecan subgroup: Yucatec Maya, Lacandon, Itza', and Mopan. Yucatecan and Cholan are the Mayan subgroups most associated with the Classic Maya hieroglyphic script.

name: Old Yucatec (Colonial Yucatec Maya)
description: The form of Yucatec Maya written in the Latin alphabet during the Spanish colonial period; the language of the Books of Chilam Balam (community chronicles blending Maya prophecy, history, and post-conquest material) and of an extensive corpus of notarial and ecclesiastical documents. The colonial Motul dictionary is a key lexical source.

name: Itza' (Itzaj)
description: Critically endangered Yucatecan Mayan language of the Itza', whose city Nojpetén (Tayasal) was the last independent Maya polity, falling to the Spanish only in 1697.

name: Proto-Cholan-Tzeltalan
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Cholan (Ch'ol, Chontal, Ch'orti', extinct Cholti) and Tzeltalan (Tzeltal, Tzotzil) subgroups. 'Classic Ch'olti'an' — the prestige language of most Classic Maya hieroglyphic inscriptions — belongs to the Cholan branch, which is why the script's language is usually identified as an ancestral Cholan variety.

name: Tzeltal
description: Major Tzeltalan Mayan language; with Tzotzil, one of the two largest Mayan languages of Chiapas. Famous in linguistics for absolute (geographic) spatial frames of reference (Brown & Levinson, Tzeltal field research).

name: Wastek (Huastec / Teenek)
region: Northern Veracruz and San Luis Potosí, Mexico (the Huasteca)
description: The most divergent Mayan language and the only one geographically separated from the main Maya area (far to the northwest). Its early split from the rest of Mayan and its isolation make Wastek crucial for Proto-Mayan reconstruction and for understanding the geographic origin of the family.

name: Colonial Quechua (Quechua General / Lengua General)
description: Standardized Quechua promoted by the Spanish colonial Church as a 'lengua general' for evangelization, codified by Domingo de Santo Tomás (1560) and the Third Council of Lima (1583). Based largely on a Southern (Cuzco / Quechua II) variety. The Huarochirí Manuscript (c. 1600), the major indigenous account of Andean religion, is in colonial Quechua.

name: Proto-Quechua I (Waywash / Central)
region: Central Peruvian highlands (Ancash, Huánuco, Junín, Lima highlands)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Quechua I (Waywash / Central) branch — the more internally diverse and probably more conservative branch, spoken in the central Peruvian highlands. The Quechua I / Quechua II split (Torero, Parker) is the primary division of the family, cross-cutting the older 'Cuzco-centric' assumptions.

name: Proto-Quechua II (Wanp'una / Peripheral)
region: Northern and southern peripheries of the Quechua area
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Quechua II (Wanp'una / Peripheral) branch, including the northern varieties (Ecuadorian Kichwa, Cajamarca, etc.) and the southern varieties (Ayacucho, Cuzco-Collao, Bolivian). The prestige Inca-era and colonial Quechua derive from Quechua IIC (southern).

name: Cuzco Quechua (Qusqu Runasimi)
description: Southern (IIC) Quechua variety of the former Inca capital; often treated as the prestige standard of southern Quechua. Famous for ejective and aspirated stop series widely argued to be the result of Aymara contact rather than inheritance.

name: Ayacucho Quechua (Chanka)
description: Southern (IIC) Quechua variety; lacks the ejective/aspirate series of Cuzco Quechua, often cited as evidence that those series are a Cuzco-Collao innovation.

name: Kichwa (Northern Quechua / Ecuadorian Quichua)
region: Ecuadorian highlands and Amazon; southern Colombia (Inga)
description: Northern (IIB) Quechua macro-variety; spread into Ecuador relatively late (largely in the Inca and early colonial periods) and underwent significant simplification of Quechua morphology. The Amazonian (Napo, Pastaza) Kichwa and highland varieties are quite distinct.

name: Ancash Quechua (Waylla Wanka / Ancash-Huailas)
description: Major Quechua I (Central) variety; among the most conservative Quechuan varieties, retaining vowel-length contrasts and archaic morphology lost in the southern prestige varieties.

name: Wanka Quechua (Huanca)
description: Highly divergent and conservative Quechua I variety; sometimes barely intelligible with southern Quechua. Its divergence is central evidence for the antiquity of the Quechua I / II split and against a simple Cuzco-origin model.

name: Classical Zapotec (Colonial Valley Zapotec)
description: Attested colonial form of Valley Zapotec, recorded in Córdova's grammar and dictionary (1578) and a large corpus of colonial notarial documents — one of the richest indigenous-language archives of colonial Mexico after Nahuatl. The pre-conquest Zapotec script (Monte Albán) is among the oldest in the Americas, though not fully deciphered.

name: Classical Mixtec (Colonial Mixtec / Ñudzahui)
description: Attested colonial form of Mixtec, recorded in the grammar of Antonio de los Reyes and the dictionary of Francisco de Alvarado (both 1593) and in colonial documents. The pre-conquest Mixtec codices (e.g. Codex Zouche-Nuttall, Codex Vindobonensis) are pictographic-logographic genealogical-historical manuscripts whose underlying language is Mixtecan.

name: Purépecha (Tarascan / P'urhépecha)
description: Language isolate of Michoacán; the language of the Tarascan state (the Purépecha Empire), the principal Mesoamerican power never conquered by the Aztec Triple Alliance (it defeated the Aztecs in the 1470s). Typologically unusual for Mesoamerica and not part of the core Mesoamerican Linguistic Area. No demonstrated relatives.

name: Loglan
region: United States (created by James Cooke Brown)
description: The first major 'logical language', devised by sociologist James Cooke Brown from 1955 to test the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis via a culturally neutral language based on predicate logic with unambiguous grammar. A 1987 copyright/control dispute led a faction to create Lojban as an independent successor; Loglan continues under the Loglan Institute.

name: Láadan
region: United States (created by Suzette Haden Elgin)
description: A feminist engineered language created by linguist and SF author Suzette Haden Elgin for her Native Tongue novels (1984), designed to test whether a language built to express women's perceptions would change speakers' experience. Features evidential and speech-act morphology and dedicated words for nuanced emotional states.

name: Toaq
description: A modern logical language (first version 2013) combining predicate-logic semantics in the Loglan/Lojban tradition with lexical tone (each root carries a tone that marks its grammatical role). Part of the 'engelang' (engineered-language) online community. (Parented to Lojban as the closest established relative in the logical-language tradition.)

name: Ithkuil
description: An extremely information-dense a priori engineered language by John Quijada (first published 2004; revised 2007, 2011, and 'New Ithkuil' in the 2020s). Designed for maximal semantic precision via elaborate morphophonology and dozens of cases. Famous as 'too complex to speak fluently'; gained attention after a 2012 New Yorker profile.

name: Kēlen
description: An artistic/engineered language notable for having no verbs — it uses a small closed set of 'relationals' to express predication, an experiment in whether a verbless language is workable. Created by Sylvia Sotomayor and well known in the conlang community; a recognized entry in the Conlang relay tradition. Fully a priori.

name: Solresol
description: An a priori auxiliary/engineered language by François Sudre in which every word is built from the seven solfège syllables (do re mi fa sol la si). Uniquely multimodal: it can be spoken, sung, played, signed, or shown as colours, making it one of the earliest cross-sensory universal languages. Detailed in Sudre's posthumous work (1866).

name: Common Eldarin
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: Tolkien's reconstructed in-universe proto-language: common ancestor of the Eldarin (Elvish) languages, descended from his Primitive Quendian. A professional philologist, Tolkien derived Quenya and Sindarin from Common Eldarin through systematic sound changes, making their relationship a genuinely worked-out genetic descent.

name: Primitive Quendian
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: Tolkien's in-universe earliest Elvish language, the ancestor (via Common Eldarin) of all later Elvish tongues, supposedly devised by the first Elves at Cuiviénen. The deepest node of Tolkien's elaborated Elvish family tree.

name: Telerin
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: An Eldarin language in Tolkien's legendarium, the tongue of the Teleri of Aman; closely related to Quenya and sometimes treated as a dialect of it. Part of the worked-out internal genealogy descending from Common Eldarin.

name: Khuzdul (Dwarvish)
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: The secret language of Tolkien's Dwarves, deliberately given a Semitic-style triconsonantal-root structure (reflecting Tolkien's analogy between Dwarves and a diaspora people). Spoken sparingly and kept secret from outsiders in-universe; only a small corpus exists (e.g. the battle cry 'Baruk Khazâd! Khazâd ai-mênu!').

name: Adûnaic
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: The language of Tolkien's Men of Númenor, also given a Semitic-influenced structure; the ancestor (with Elvish admixture) of the Westron 'Common Speech' of Middle-earth. Developed in detail in 'Lowdham's Report' within The Notion Club Papers.

name: Black Speech
region: England (created by J. R. R. Tolkien)
description: The language devised by Sauron for Mordor in Tolkien's legendarium, intended to be deliberately harsh; the Ring inscription ('Ash nazg durbatulûk...') is its most famous specimen. Only fragments exist; an 'orkish' debased form is referenced in-universe.

name: Dothraki
region: United States (created by David J. Peterson for HBO)
description: Constructed language created by David J. Peterson (selected via a Language Creation Society competition) for HBO's Game of Thrones, expanded from the handful of words in George R. R. Martin's novels into a full language with several thousand words and complete grammar. One of the most prominent examples of professional conlanging for screen media.

name: High Valyrian
region: United States (created by David J. Peterson for HBO)
description: Constructed language created by David J. Peterson for HBO's Game of Thrones, conceived as a prestige/classical language (analogous to Latin) with living descendant 'Low Valyrian' / Bastard Valyrian varieties of Slaver's Bay — i.e. Peterson built it diachronically with daughter languages. Later offered as a course on Duolingo.

name: Na'vi
region: United States (created by Paul Frommer for the film Avatar)
description: Constructed language created by linguist Paul Frommer for James Cameron's Avatar films, spoken by the Na'vi of Pandora. Features typologically unusual but human-pronounceable elements (ejectives, an infix-heavy verb morphology, a tripartite case system). Has an active learner community.

name: Proto-South Dravidian (Proto-South Dravidian I)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the South Dravidian (SDr I) branch: Tamil-Kannada (Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Kodava, Toda, Kota, Irula, Badaga) and Tulu. The South Dravidian / South-Central Dravidian split is the primary cleavage in the southern part of the family.

name: Proto-Tamil-Kannada
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tamil-Kannada subgroup, splitting into Tamil-Malayalam (Tamil-Kodagu) and Kannada-Badaga. The literary languages Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam all descend from this node; their early divergence underlies the long separate literary histories of Tamil and Kannada.

name: Proto-South-Central Dravidian (Proto-South Dravidian II)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the South-Central Dravidian (SDr II) branch: Telugu, Gondi, Konda, Kui, Kuvi, Pengo, Manda, Koya. Notable for the 'apical displacement' sound change. Telugu is by far the largest member and the most-spoken Dravidian language after no other (it ranks among the most-spoken languages of India).

name: Proto-Central Dravidian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Central Dravidian branch: Kolami, Naiki, Parji, Ollari, Gadaba (Dravidian). Small, mostly tribal languages of central India.

name: Proto-North Dravidian
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the North Dravidian branch: Kurukh (Oraon), Malto, and the far-flung Brahui of Balochistan. Brahui's position — a Dravidian outlier some 1,500 km from the main area — is debated: it may be a relic of a wider Dravidian distribution or a later migration, bearing on theories of a Dravidian/Indus presence in the northwest.

name: Old Kannada (Halegannada)
description: Earliest attested stage of Kannada; the Halmidi inscription (c. 450 CE) is the oldest full Kannada inscription. Old Kannada was the court language of the Kadamba, Chalukya, and Rashtrakuta dynasties and of foundational works including the Kavirajamarga (c. 850) and the 'three gems' Pampa, Ponna, and Ranna (10th c.).

name: Kodava (Coorgi)
description: South Dravidian language of the Kodava people; sometimes treated as closer to Tamil-Malayalam, sometimes to Kannada. Written in the Kannada script.

name: Toda
description: South Dravidian language of the pastoralist Toda community of the Nilgiris; famous in phonetics for an exceptionally large consonant inventory and a rich set of trills/fricatives, documented by M. B. Emeneau. Severely endangered.

name: Kota
description: South Dravidian language of the Kota community of the Nilgiris, neighbours of the Toda; documented by Emeneau. Endangered.

name: Badaga
description: South Dravidian language closely related to Kannada; the Badaga are the largest indigenous group of the Nilgiris.

name: Irula
region: Nilgiri foothills, Tamil Nadu and Kerala
description: South Dravidian language transitional between Tamil and the Nilgiri languages; the Irula are well known for traditional snake- and rat-catching expertise.

name: Middle Tamil
description: Intermediate stage between Old Tamil (Sangam-era) and Modern Tamil; the language of the Chola imperial epigraphy, the Bhakti devotional corpus (Tevaram, Nalayira Divya Prabandham), and Kamban's Ramavataram (12th c.). Diglossia between literary and spoken Tamil deepened in this period.

name: Old Telugu
description: Earliest attested stage of Telugu; the first full Telugu inscriptions date to the 6th–7th c. (the Erragudi and later Renati Chola inscriptions), with the literary tradition beginning with Nannaya's Mahabharatamu (11th c.). Telugu developed its own Brahmi-derived script, shared in origin with Kannada (the Kannada-Telugu script).

name: Kui
description: South-Central Dravidian language of the Kondh people; historically associated (in colonial accounts) with the meriah human-sacrifice rites suppressed by the British in the 19th century.

name: Konda (Kubi)
description: Conservative South-Central Dravidian language important for reconstruction; retains features lost in Telugu.

name: Kolami
description: Largest Central Dravidian language; documented by Emeneau in a classic descriptive grammar (1955).

name: Parji
description: Central Dravidian language of the Bastar tribal region.

name: Kurukh (Oraon)
region: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal; tea regions of Assam and Bangladesh
description: Largest North Dravidian language; the language of the Oraon (Kurukh) people. A Dravidian island surrounded by Indo-Aryan and Munda languages. The Tolong Siki script was devised for it in the 20th century. Closely related to Malto and (more distantly) Brahui.

name: Malto (Paharia)
description: North Dravidian language of the Sauria and Mal Paharia communities of the Rajmahal Hills; closely related to Kurukh.

name: Proto-Kra-Dai (Proto-Tai-Kadai, alt. id)
region: Southern China (probably around the Pearl/Lingnan region or further south)
description: Alias node for the Kra-Dai (Tai-Kadai, Daic) family root. Comprises Kra, Kam-Sui, Hlai, Be, and the large Tai branch. Increasingly argued to be related to Austronesian (the 'Austro-Tai' hypothesis, revived by Sagart and Ostapirat), with Kra-Dai as a sister or offshoot of an early Austronesian-related group on the south Chinese mainland.

name: Proto-Tai
region: Northern Vietnam / Guangxi region (probable Tai homeland)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Tai branch — the largest Kra-Dai branch and the only one with major national languages. Splits into Northern Tai (Zhuang, Bouyei, Saek), Central Tai (Nung, Tay), and Southwestern Tai (Thai, Lao, Shan, Ahom, etc.). The Southwestern dispersal into Thailand, Laos, and Assam is largely a second-millennium-CE event.

name: Proto-Southwestern Tai
region: Upland southeastern Asia (around the China–Vietnam–Laos borderlands)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Southwestern Tai languages, which spread rapidly across mainland Southeast Asia in the late first and the second millennium CE, displacing or assimilating Mon, Khmer, and Austroasiatic upland populations. Includes Thai, Lao, Shan, Tai Lü, Tai Dam, Tai Khün, Ahom, and others.

name: Proto-Northern Tai
description: Reconstructed ancestor of Northern Tai: the northern Zhuang varieties, Bouyei, and the conservative Saek.

name: Tai Lü (Lue / Xishuangbanna Dai)
description: Southwestern Tai language of the Tai Lü; the language of the historic polity of Sipsongpanna (Xishuangbanna). Written in the Tham (Dharma) and New Tai Lue scripts.

name: Tai Dam (Black Tai)
region: Northwestern Vietnam, Laos; diaspora in Thailand, France, US
description: Southwestern Tai language of the Black Tai; written in its own Tai Viet script. Resisted lowland Buddhist and Lao political domination, retaining a distinct animist-influenced culture.

name: Ahom
description: Extinct Southwestern Tai language of the Ahom, who founded the Ahom kingdom that ruled Assam for ~600 years (1228–1826) after migrating from upper Burma/Yunnan. Preserved as a liturgical/ritual language in its own Ahom script (the buranji chronicles); the spoken language was replaced by Assamese. Subject of modern revival interest.

name: Nung (Nùng)
description: Central Tai language closely related to Tay and southern Zhuang; one of the larger minority languages of Vietnam.

name: Tay (Tày / Thổ)
description: Central Tai language; the Tày are the largest ethnic minority in Vietnam. Historically written in a Chinese-character-based script (Chữ Nôm Tày).

name: Bouyei (Buyi / Zhongjia)
description: Northern Tai language closely related to (northern) Zhuang; the Bouyei are one of China's recognized nationalities.

name: Saek
region: Central Laos and adjacent Thailand (Nakhon Phanom)
description: Highly conservative Northern Tai language geographically displaced far to the south among Southwestern Tai speakers; important for Tai reconstruction because it preserves archaic consonant clusters and a more complex tone system.

name: Proto-Kam-Sui
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kam-Sui branch of Kra-Dai: Kam (Dong), Sui, Mulam, Maonan, Then. Kam-Sui languages have some of the largest tone inventories in the world (up to ~15 tones counting checked syllables).

name: Kam (Dong / Gaeml)
description: Largest Kam-Sui language; the Kam (Dong) are famous for polyphonic 'Grand Song' (Kgal Laox) choral singing, inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list (2009), and for their wooden drum-towers and wind-and-rain bridges.

name: Sui (Shui)
description: Kam-Sui language; notable for the Shui (Sui) logographic ritual script (shuishu), used by ritual specialists, with characters partly resembling reversed or modified Chinese characters.

name: Maonan
description: Kam-Sui language of the Maonan nationality.

name: Proto-Kra (Proto-Geyang)
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Kra (Geyang/Kadai) branch — the branch whose name gives the 'Kra' of 'Kra-Dai'. Small, scattered, mostly endangered languages: Gelao, Lachi, Buyang, Pubiao (Laqua), Qabiao. Ostapirat's work on Kra was central to establishing the family's internal structure and the Kra-Dai/Austronesian comparison.

name: Gelao (Klau)
description: Kra language; highly endangered and fragmented into several divergent varieties, though the Gelao are a fairly populous official nationality in China (most no longer speak the language).

name: Buyang
description: Kra language important for the Austro-Tai hypothesis: Buyang numerals and basic vocabulary show some of the clearest resemblances to Austronesian, central to Sagart's and Ostapirat's arguments.

name: Proto-Hlai
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Hlai (Li) languages of Hainan, the indigenous languages of the island predating Chinese settlement. Hlai is a relatively early offshoot within Kra-Dai.

name: Hlai (Li)
description: Main Hlai language; the Li are the indigenous people of Hainan. A Latin-based orthography was created in 1957.

name: Be (Ong Be / Lingao)
description: Kra-Dai language of uncertain internal position (sometimes grouped with Tai, sometimes treated as a primary branch), spoken near Haikou on Hainan. Heavily influenced by Chinese.

name: Proto-Malayic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Malayic subgroup, including Malay (and its standardized national forms Indonesian/Malaysian), Minangkabau, Banjar, Iban, Kerinci, and many local Malay varieties. The Malayic homeland is debated between western Borneo and Sumatra. Old Malay is attested from the 7th c. (Srivijaya inscriptions).

name: Old Malay
region: Sumatra, Malay Peninsula, western Java (Srivijaya and successors)
description: Earliest attested stage of Malay, recorded in 7th-century Srivijayan inscriptions (Kedukan Bukit, 683 CE; Talang Tuo; Kota Kapur) in a Pallava-derived script, with heavy Sanskrit borrowing. Old Malay was a court and trade language across maritime Southeast Asia and is the ancestor of Classical Malay and the modern national standards.

name: Classical Malay
region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, maritime Southeast Asia
description: The Malay of the Islamic sultanates (Malacca, Aceh, Johor, Riau), written in the Arabic-derived Jawi script. The lingua franca of maritime trade across the archipelago and the basis from which both standard Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) and standard Malaysian (Bahasa Melayu) were later codified.

name: Minangkabau
region: West Sumatra, Indonesia; diaspora across the archipelago (notably Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia)
description: Malayic language closely related to Malay; the language of the Minangkabau, the world's largest matrilineal society. Minangkabau merantau (out-migration) traditions carried the language and culture across Southeast Asia.

name: Banjar (Banjarese)
region: South Kalimantan, Indonesia; diaspora in Sumatra and Malaysia
description: Malayic language of the Banjar people, with a Dayak (Barito) substrate; a regional lingua franca of southeastern Borneo and a trade language.

name: Iban (Sea Dayak)
description: Malayic language; the largest indigenous (Dayak) language of Sarawak. Historically associated with the 'Sea Dayak' and their riverine and coastal raiding/trading networks. Rich oral literature (the epic timang and pantun traditions).

name: Kerinci
description: Highly distinctive Malayic language famous for complex word-final alternations ('phrasal alternation' / absolute vs. oblique word forms) unusual within Malayic.

name: Proto-Chamic
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Chamic languages — the principal Austronesian languages of mainland Southeast Asia, brought by seafarers to the Vietnamese coast. Includes Cham, Jarai, Rade, Chru, Roglai, Haroi, and Tsat. Chamic is the textbook case of Austronesian languages becoming 'Mon-Khmer-like' through intense mainland contact.

name: Cham
region: Coastal Vietnam and Cambodia (Mekong delta, Tonlé Sap)
description: Principal Chamic language; the language of Champa, the Austronesian kingdom that dominated central Vietnam from c. 192 CE until its absorption by Vietnam in 1832. The Đông Yên Châu inscription (c. 4th c. CE) is the oldest attested Austronesian text. Written historically in a Brahmi-derived Cham script; Eastern and Western Cham now diverge.

name: Jarai
region: Central Highlands of Vietnam (Gia Lai) and adjacent Cambodia
description: Largest Chamic language of the Central Highlands ('Montagnard'); the Jarai retained a traditional 'Pötao' (master-of-fire/water) ritual institution.

name: Rade (Ede)
region: Đắk Lắk, Central Highlands of Vietnam
description: Major Chamic language of the matrilineal Ede people; one of the better-documented Highland languages with a Latin-based orthography from the French period.

name: Tsat (Utsul / Hainan Cham)
description: Chamic language of the Utsul, Muslim refugees from Champa who settled on Hainan. Tsat is fully tonal — a dramatic example of an Austronesian language acquiring a Sinitic/Mon-Khmer-style tone system through contact; much cited in tonogenesis research.

name: Acehnese (Aceh)
description: Aceh-Chamic Austronesian language; together with Chamic forms an 'Aceh-Chamic' subgroup, indicating a historical link between Aceh and the mainland Cham. The language of the Aceh Sultanate, a major Islamic power and the center of long anti-colonial resistance (the Aceh War, 1873–1914).

name: Proto-Batak
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the Batak languages of the North Sumatran highlands: Toba, Karo, Simalungun, Pakpak (Dairi), Angkola, and Mandailing. The Batak peoples used the Brahmi-derived Batak script (surat Batak), traditionally for ritual and divination texts (pustaha).

name: Toba Batak
region: Lake Toba region, North Sumatra, Indonesia
description: Largest Batak language; written historically in the Batak script and now in Latin.

name: Karo Batak
description: Northern Batak language, fairly divergent from Toba Batak.

name: Nias
region: Nias Island, off western Sumatra, Indonesia
description: Austronesian language of Nias island; notable for having open syllables only (every word ends in a vowel) and an unusual ergative-like case system marked by initial-consonant mutation. The Nias are known for megalithic culture and stone-jumping (fahombo).

name: Proto-South Sulawesi
description: Reconstructed ancestor of the South Sulawesi subgroup: Buginese, Makassarese, Toraja-Sa'dan, Mandar, and others. Speakers developed the Lontara (Bugis-Makassar) script, a Brahmi descendant.

name: Buginese (Bugis)
region: South Sulawesi, Indonesia; maritime diaspora across the archipelago
description: Major South Sulawesi language; the seafaring Bugis spread across maritime Southeast Asia. Written in the Lontara script. The Bugis epic 'La Galigo' (Sureq Galigo) is one of the largest literary works in the world by volume.

name: Makassarese (Makasar)
description: Major South Sulawesi language; the language of the Gowa-Tallo (Makassar) sultanate, a dominant 16th–17th-century maritime power. Written in the Lontara script.

name: Toraja-Sa'dan (Toraja)
region: Tana Toraja highlands, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
description: South Sulawesi language of the Toraja, internationally known for elaborate funerary rites, cliff-burials with tau-tau effigies, and tongkonan houses.
